results.title: Automated Grading of Handwritten Mathematics Using Vision-Capable LLMs (Levine, Aenlle, Zilles, West, Silva; UIUC)
results.snippet: arXiv, 18 May 2026. GPT-5-mini, GPT-5.1 and Gemini-3-flash grade handwritten maths straight from the page image against instructor rubrics (numerical methods n=440 students, dynamics n=245) in one call that transcribes and grades together; the authors cite prior work saying this beats separate transcribe-then-grade, but give no head-to-head numbers of their own. Rubric-item accuracy about 87-99% (Gemini-3-flash 89% to over 99%, GPT-5.1 87-95%). Transcription failures cause 71-100% of errors across models (87% for the best model), not rubric misapplication; other failures: blurry or rotated photos, hallucinated text that is not on the page, incomplete work marked correct, equivalent expressions mis-simplified. Leniency: Gemini-3-flash makes about 2.5 false positives (marks wrongly given) per false negative, GPT models are near parity. Authors judge accuracy adequate for low-stakes formative feedback, not high-stakes use. ExamLeaf takeaway: cheap flash/mini vision models are close to usable on maths, but the bottleneck is reading the handwriting, and leniency is model-specific.

results.title: Vision-Language Models for Criterion-Level Grading of Handwritten Examinations in Outcome-Based Education (Tonmoy, Ahmed, Syfullah, Alam)
results.snippet: arXiv, 13-15 Sep 2026. 485 scanned undergraduate exam answers (nine subjects, 1,982 rubric-criterion records; funded by the Bangladesh Accreditation Council; answer language not stated) graded by open-weight VLMs. Chinese Qwen2.5-VL: zero-shot QWK 0.599 / MAE 0.664 marks; after LoRA fine-tuning on the rubric data QWK 0.727 / MAE 0.435 marks against the examiner, versus mean human-to-human QWK 0.551. InternVL3 0.707, Pixtral 0.659, OCR-free Donut baseline only 0.080. Aggregate bias near zero (+0.014 marks), but repeatability was poor: at temperature 0.7, 50.2-63.6% of criteria changed marks across five runs (exact repeatability 36.4-49.8%, ICC 0.79-0.87). Authors advise deterministic decoding for reported marks, rubric-specific calibration, criterion-level records kept for teacher review, and separate validation of the model's explanations. ExamLeaf takeaway: best evidence that a fine-tuned Chinese open-weight VLM can reach examiner-level QWK, and that repeat-run instability must be controlled.

results.title: Large-scale AI grading of handwritten physics assessments: Score agreement and Olympiad team selection outcomes (Pathak et al.)
results.snippet: arXiv, Aug 2026. GPT-5.5 graded 10,364 scanned handwritten pages (520 submissions: national Physics Olympiad theory, final selection with experiments, a university quantum-mechanics exam). Total-score Pearson r 0.91-0.97 with official marks, but exact agreement on individual question parts only 63% in round 1, rising to 70% in round 2 after rubric refinement and page-by-page grading; within +/-0.5 point 79% to 84%. The AI over-awarded relative to examiners in every round-1 total-score comparison (OE1 +5.9%, quantum exam +9.3% of max, falling to +2.2% and -0.1% in round 2); partial credit, rubric-specific diagram features and judging whether data, fit and conclusion cohere were hardest. Confidence flags help (mean absolute difference about 5-10% of max for high-confidence parts versus 17-28% for medium/low) but auto-accepting all 1,724 high-confidence parts would still pass 87 (about 5%) that differed from the official mark by more than one point. Authors: use as a second reader or audit tool under examiner control, with an explicit rubric. ExamLeaf takeaway: confidence thresholds reduce but do not remove error; a detailed marking scheme is the main lever.

results.title: EDU-CIRCUIT-HW: Evaluating Multimodal Large Language Models on Real-World University-Level STEM Student Handwritten Solutions (ACL 2026 Findings)
results.snippet: arXiv Jan 2026. 1,300+ authentic handwritten university circuit-homework solutions graded by six multimodal models, including Chinese Qwen3-VL-Plus and Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking alongside Gemini-3-Pro-Preview, Gemini-2.5-Pro, GPT-5.1 and Claude-4.5-Sonnet. Key warning: even the strongest model misreads the work in 37.62% of samples, yet only 7.60% of recognition errors change the grade (error impact rate), so a plausible mark can hide a misread answer ('latent failures'). Feeding expert transcriptions to the grader gives 89.47% binary agreement, well above what any model reaches reading the handwriting itself; models match humans on right/wrong agreement but lag on stricter point-level agreement. A hybrid design that routes only 3.3% of assignments to human graders lifted point agreement from 69.91% to 74.42% (Gemini-2.5-Pro) and 66.87% to 75.76% (GPT-5.1). ExamLeaf takeaway: grade accuracy alone hides recognition failures, so log what the model read and route low-confidence sheets to teachers.

results.title: Evaluating Vision-Language and Large Language Models for Automated Student Assessment in Indonesian Classrooms (Aisyah, Kautsar, Hidayat, Chowdhury, Koto)
results.snippet: arXiv, June 2025, revised April 2026. 646 handwritten answer sheets (14,000+ answers) from six Indonesian primary schools (414 urban, 232 rural sheets), Grade-4 maths and English: the closest school-level, developing-country match to ExamLeaf in this search. GPT-4o reads the handwriting (Chinese Qwen-VL-72B was tried as OCR and judged 'suboptimal'), then GPT-4o, Llama-3.1-70B, Qwen2.5-72B and DeepSeek-Chat grade the text. Mean absolute error on a 0-100 scale ranged from about 1.5 to 18.7 by question type and model; swapping OCR output for human transcripts cut GPT-4o English short-answer error from 14.6 to 9.2 (OCR errors propagate into marks), and DeepSeek reached 0.8 total MAE on maths with clean transcripts. Fairness warning: English grading error with human transcripts was 0.8 for urban schools versus 23.1 for rural schools, which the authors tie to variation in writing style and grammar. ExamLeaf takeaway: Chinese text LLMs can grade clean text competitively, but messy student handwriting and regional writing styles drive unequal error.

results.title: Lower-Resource, Higher Scores: Language Bias in LLM Evaluators (Zhou, Resck, Hui, Korhonen)
results.snippet: arXiv, 16 July 2026 (final version 26 Aug 2026). Tests whether LLM judges score identical content differently by language: semantically identical instruction-response pairs in 23 languages (Hindi is the only Indian language; Bengali and Assamese were not tested) rated by eight open-weight evaluators (Aya Expanse 32B, Qwen2.5-72B, Llama-3.1-70B, M-Prometheus-14B plus four reward models). Lower-resource languages are scored systematically higher, i.e. more leniently: about 0.4-0.5 points on a 1-5 scale (Hindi about 3.7 versus English/French/Italian about 3.2), Spearman -0.81 against language resource level, up to 43% difference in acceptance rate under a single global threshold, with the effect stronger when the model is less confident. Per-language thresholds help but need language identification, which code-switched text can defeat. Caveat: this is chat/safety/reasoning judging, not exam marking, but it is the closest published evidence that an AI marker may be more lenient on Hindi (and likely Assamese or Bengali) answers than on English ones, so calibrate and audit marks per language.

results.title: OpenRouter public model catalogue API (prices, context, modalities, per-model providers)
results.snippet: Primary source, 466 models, queried 2026-10-08. USD per 1M input/output tokens (ctx). Chinese vision-capable: Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct 0.21/1.90 (131k-262k; cheapest endpoint DeepInfra 0.20/0.88), Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B 0.15/0.60, Qwen3-VL-8B 0.117/0.455, Qwen3.5-Flash 0.065/0.26 (1M), GLM-4.6V 0.30/0.90 (131k; only Z.AI and Novita), GLM-5.3-Flash 0.15/0.50 (1M), DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 0.30/1.20 (:batch 0.112/0.336; DeepSeek's own endpoint 0.15/0.60), Kimi K2.5 0.45/2.25 and K2.6 0.465/2.45 (original K2 is text-only), MiniMax M3 0.30/1.20, MiMo-V2.6-Flash 0.14/0.28. Western: Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite 0.10/0.40 (1M; :batch 0.05/0.20), Gemini 2.5 Flash 0.30/2.50 (:batch 0.15/1.25), GPT-5 mini 0.25/2.00 (400k; :batch 0.125/1.00), Claude Haiku 4.5 1.00/5.00, Claude Haiku 5.5 0.10/0.50 (added 2026-10-07, unproven). No separate per-image fee: images bill as input tokens (Gemini's pricing.image equals its token rate). Indian: sarvamai/sarvam-m (24B, text-only, 32k) exists as a stub with zero live endpoints; no Sarvam model is routable. Per-model provider lists: /api/v1/models/{id}/endpoints. Fees per openrouter.ai/docs/faq: no inference markup, 5.5% ($0.80 min) on card credit purchases, prompts not logged by default.

results.title: OpenRouter docs: Provider Routing (only, ignore, order, allow_fallbacks, data_collection, zdr)
results.snippet: Defines how to restrict which providers see student images: provider object fields order, only, ignore, allow_fallbacks (default true), require_parameters, data_collection (allow|deny, default allow), zdr, sort, quantizations, max_price. Pin to approved providers with only plus allow_fallbacks:false. In-region routing exists only for the EU and US (eu./us.openrouter.ai, Business and Enterprise plans); the page has no India region, so Indian data residency cannot come from OpenRouter alone (implies direct India-region API or self-hosting for DPDP-sensitive paths).

results.title: OpenRouter docs: Zero Data Retention (ZDR) enforcement
results.snippet: ZDR can be enforced in account privacy settings (global or per model group), in guardrails per API key, or per request with provider.zdr=true (can only tighten). Live ZDR endpoint list at /api/v1/endpoints/zdr (942 endpoints on 2026-10-08): Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B has ZDR endpoints at DeepInfra, Novita, Parasail, Venice (not Alibaba's own); GLM-4.6V at Z.AI and Novita; GLM-5.3-Flash at about 25 providers; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at 21; Gemini 2.5 Flash/Flash-Lite only via Google; GPT-5 mini only via Azure; Claude Haiku 5.5 via Bedrock. In-memory prompt caching is not counted as retention; ZDR does not cover plugins/tools such as web search. ZDR concerns storage, not location, so it does not by itself give Indian data residency.

results.title: Sarvam AI API pricing (INR): LLM tokens, Document AI per page, translation, dubbing
results.snippet: Official Indian-provider price list, read raw on 2026-10-08. LLMs per 1M tokens in/out: Sarvam 105B Rs 29.28/73.20 (cached input Rs 10.98), Gemma-4 31B Rs 36.60/91.50, GLM 5.2 Rs 128.10/402.60; Sarvam-M is no longer listed. Document AI: Rs 0.50/page digitisation, Rs 1.00/page extraction (about Rs 6-12 for a 12-page paper; handwriting support is not claimed in the Sarvam Vision docs, which list Assamese, Bengali and Hindi among 22 Indian languages). Translation Rs 0.004-0.005 per character, so about Rs 10 to translate 2,000 characters of feedback, far above LLM token cost for the same text; dubbing Rs 1.20-1.67 per second.

claims.claim: A Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct model fine-tuned with LoRA on 1,483 criterion marks from one examiner graded handwritten undergraduate answers directly from page images (no OCR step). On 291 held-out criterion judgments from 72 answers it reached QWK 0.727 and MAE 0.435 marks against that examiner (60.8% exact match, 93.8% within one mark). Mean QWK among three human markers (the examiner plus two independent faculty) was 0.551. The authors say this reflects calibration to the examiner's training marks, so it shows the model reproducing one marker's style, not beating independent examiners.
claims.quote: [Paraphrase, no verbatim quote; see arXiv 2609.14284v2: abstract (QWK 0.727, MAE 0.435, human-pair QWK 0.551, calibration caveat), Table VI, Study 2 in Sec. V-C and Table IX]

claims.claim: Calibration, not prompting, produced the gain. Untuned zero-shot Qwen2.5-VL scored QWK 0.599, MAE 0.664, exact match 28.5%, and over-awarded by +0.205 marks on average. Few-shot examples lowered QWK in every configuration that produced valid scores (by 0.005 to 0.051). LoRA raised QWK by 0.128 to 0.200 over zero-shot for Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B and Pixtral-12B, and beat partial fine-tuning for all three. The small OCR-free Donut baseline gave usable marks for only about 52% of criteria even after adaptation.
claims.quote: [Paraphrase, no verbatim quote; see arXiv 2609.14284v2: Table VI, Table VII and Study 1 text in Sec. V-B]

claims.claim: Marks were not repeatable under sampling. Re-running each LoRA-tuned model five times at temperature 0.7 (only the decoding seed varied) gave high ICC(2,1) (0.790 Qwen2.5-VL, 0.874 InternVL3, 0.862 Pixtral), yet only 36.4% to 49.8% of the 291 criteria got an identical mark in all five runs (41.9% for Qwen2.5-VL), so 50.2% to 63.6% changed. Mean per-item standard deviation was 0.25 to 0.32 marks. The authors recommend greedy decoding for reported marks and note that training and numerical reproducibility still need separate checks.
claims.quote: Tonmoy et al., arXiv 2609.14284 abstract: "50.2-63.6% of criteria changed marks across five sampled runs"

claims.claim: The study cannot settle two open questions for ExamLeaf. It says it does not measure transcription loss or compare against an OCR-plus-text-grader pipeline, so it gives no single-step versus two-step evidence. Its corpus is 485 scanned undergraduate scripts (9 subjects, 12 question templates, 47 rubric criteria; mostly prose, some tables, equations, diagrams and code), marked by one examiner. The answer language/script is not stated and no Bengali, Assamese or Hindi was evaluated. Pages were stitched per answer at 200 DPI and downsized to a 1,280 px long side (768 px for Pixtral). Transfer to unseen templates or institutions was not tested.
claims.quote: [Paraphrase, no verbatim quote; see arXiv 2609.14284v2: Sec. II-A (no OCR-plus-grader comparison), Sec. IV-A corpus, Table III, Table V, Sec. V-H scope and limitations]

claims.claim: Errors clustered in identifiable places, which supports risk-based teacher review. For the LoRA Qwen2.5-VL system, MAE rose with criterion weight (0.267 marks for criteria worth up to 2, 0.375 for 2 to 3, 0.598 above 3). Subject MAE ranged from 0.125 (Fisheries, prose) to 1.625 (Object-Oriented Programming, code, only 20 test judgments). 6.2% of marks differed from the examiner by more than one mark even though overall signed bias was just +0.014. Attention-map explanations were no more faithful than random masking, and four faculty reviewers did not agree on their usefulness (ICC about -0.03; only 33% would adopt with teacher override).
claims.quote: [Paraphrase, no verbatim quote; see arXiv 2609.14284v2: Study 4 in Sec. V-E with Table XI and Fig. 7, Study 5 in Sec. V-F with Tables XII and XIII]

claims.claim: Single-call photo grading (one LLM call does both transcription and rubric scoring, no separate OCR step) on 600 photographed student submissions to 5 open-ended university STEM problems matched instructor rubric-item decisions 89-99% of the time per question for Gemini-3-flash (authors' headline: 95% overall; my pooled recomputation from Table 1: about 94%), versus 89-98% for GPT-5-mini and 87-95% for GPT-5.1. Gemini was best or tied-best on every question, but its edge over GPT-5-mini is only 0-2 points per question (no confidence intervals or significance tests reported), the full-size GPT-5.1 scored below GPT-5-mini on all five questions, and Gemini's two weakest results (89% and 93%) were the proctored exam photos taken with document cameras.
claims.quote: [Paraphrase, not verbatim] Table 1, %RIA as Gemini-3-flash / GPT-5-mini / GPT-5.1: C1-Q1 96/95/87; C1-Q2 99/98/95; C1-Q3 99/97/94; C2-Q1 89/89/88; C2-Q2 93/92/88 (submissions 55/69/122/242/112); Sec. 4 states 95% for Gemini 3 Flash.

claims.claim: Most grading errors in photo-based grading are reading errors, not rubric-logic errors: the authors report that 87% of the best model's (Gemini-3-flash) disagreements with the human grader were transcription failures (missed, hallucinated or mistranscribed writing), leaving 13% rubric misapplication, versus about 28% rubric errors for the GPT models. Transcription was at least 70% of errors in every question/model pair except C1-Q1 with GPT-5.1 (24%), where the model failed to accept a sign-flipped answer that the rubric explicitly allowed. Caveat from my recomputation of Table 1: 87% is close to the unweighted mean of Gemini's five per-question transcription shares (92, 100, 100, 71, 75 = 87.6); weighting by error counts gives roughly 75%, so the headline overstates the pooled share, although the conclusion that transcription dominates stands.
claims.quote: "attributable to transcription failures rather than rubric misapplication" (Levine et al., arXiv:2605.19043, abstract)

claims.claim: Vision grading tends to hallucinate in the student's favour when handwriting is hard to read: Gemini-3-flash's errors skewed toward false positives (marks the human did not award) at 2.5 to 1, with the authors saying it occasionally hallucinated correct answers while struggling to interpret handwriting; hallucinated text sometimes resembled the reference solution and inflated scores, mostly on blurry or rotated images; GPT models showed near parity of false positives and negatives. The authors found no consistent leniency or strictness pattern by question or model, so no review-flagging rule emerged and they call for further study. Other recorded failures: solutions marked correct when only a subset of required rubric elements was present despite accurate transcription, and mishandled equivalent answers (for example rounded decimals versus exact fractions).
claims.quote: [Paraphrase, not verbatim] Sec. 3.1 (blurry, rotated, hallucinated-text, missing-elements and equivalent-expression failure modes), Sec. 3 (no consistent false-positive/false-negative pattern by question or model), Sec. 4 (2.5-to-1 false-positive skew for Gemini 3 Flash; GPT near parity).

claims.claim: The authors rate even the best model (Gemini-3-flash) as adequate only for low-stakes, formative feedback shown with a warning that it may contain mistakes; high-stakes marking needs more reliability. Their deployed design is asynchronous grading after submissions close, with human review and override and human grades always taking precedence; proposed mitigations are student-side preview/crop and quality checks, preview transcriptions, several capture modes including direct file upload, and model-controlled rotation (at extra token cost). Cited second-hand: Kortemeyer et al. (arXiv:2510.05162, GPT-5 on calculus exam scans) found unfiltered AI only adequate for low-stakes feedback (R2 = 0.85 vs TA grades), and a confidence-based human-in-the-loop variant needed manual review of 70% of items (the text prints R2 = 0.85 for both variants, an apparent typo).
claims.quote: [Paraphrase, not verbatim] Sec. 2 (asynchronous grading; human override takes precedence), Sec. 3.1 (mitigations: quality review, preview transcriptions, upload modes, rotation tools), Sec. 4 (low-stakes verdict), Sec. 1 (summary of Kortemeyer et al. [2]).

claims.claim: Limits on applying these numbers to ExamLeaf: (a) the paper runs no head-to-head of single-call versus separate OCR-then-grade; it relies on its authors' own 2-page SIGCSE 2026 paper [4] for that and cites older results (Liu et al. 2024: about 60% grading accuracy for GPT-4V/MathPix transcription plus GPT-4 rubric checks; Wang et al. 2025: purpose-built formula recognisers beat GPT-4o, before Gemini 3); (b) only GPT-5-mini, GPT-5.1 and Gemini-3-flash were tested, with no Chinese, open-weight or dedicated OCR baselines; (c) it covers only US university numerical-methods and dynamics problems and reports nothing on Indic scripts, other languages, chemistry or school exams; (d) students photographed single questions (5-9 rubric items each) and could preview, crop and resubmit, which the authors say may contribute to the higher accuracy, unlike unreviewed phone photos of 12-page papers; (e) ground truth came from instructors who were also the study authors, with no inter-rater agreement reported; (f) no dollar cost, latency or image-token figures are given, only a statement that per-token costs make production use feasible; (g) it is an arXiv v1 preprint whose listing says it will appear at AIED 2026.
claims.quote: [Paraphrase, not verbatim] Sec. 1 (Our-work-differs paragraph; Liu et al. [6]; Wang et al. [11]), Sec. 2 (single-call motivated by [4]; three models tested; instructors graded ground truth; randomised problems), Sec. 3.1 and Sec. 4 (no cost or latency data); arXiv abstract page Comments field (AIED 2026).

claims.claim: Single-step multimodal grading tracked examiner totals closely. Pathak et al. (arXiv preprint v1, 20 Aug 2026) had GPT-5.5 (Thinking, high effort) grade handwritten scans directly from page images, given the questions, solutions, official rubrics and anonymized scans; no OCR stage is described (OCR appears only in the related-work text). Over 520 submissions, 10,364 scanned pages and 416 students (national Physics Olympiad theory exam, selection camp, university quantum-mechanics exam), AI totals correlated with official totals at Pearson r 0.91-0.97 in Round I and 0.93-0.96 in Round II. Round II total-score mean absolute difference was 3.8-5.1% of maximum marks. The five students the AI ranked highest were exactly the five chosen by official grading (order differed). The reference was moderated official marks, and no human-human regrading baseline was run.
claims.quote: [Paraphrase only, to respect the one-quote limit] Locator: abstract and Sec. III, Fig. 1 (r by exam, Round II MAD 4.8%, 5.1%, 4.2%, 3.8%); Sec. III team-selection paragraph; Sec. II.2 grading procedure.

claims.claim: The AI grader was systematically lenient (Pathak et al., arXiv:2608.20521). In Round I the mean AI-minus-official total was positive for all four assessments (+9.3% of maximum marks on the 40-script quantum-mechanics exam, +5.9% on the 350-script Olympiad theory exam). At question-part level the bias was largest for conceptual written reasoning (+13.3% in Round I, +4.3% in Round II). The authors list as recurring failures that the AI gives partial credit to work examiners scored zero when it looks superficially plausible, and gives too much credit to a correct-looking final answer despite flawed reasoning. The revised Round II cut total bias to +2.2% (Olympiad theory) and -0.1% (quantum mechanics), but the two selection-camp components still sat at +4.0% to +4.5%. Leniency was reduced, not removed.
claims.quote: "plausible symbols, text, tables, or diagram features" (Pathak et al., arXiv:2608.20521, Sec. IV.4, table of recurring sources of disagreement)

claims.claim: Per-question marks agree far less than totals, and partial credit is the weak spot. Over 7,058 official question parts the AI matched the examiner's mark exactly about 63% of the time in Round I and about 70% in Round II, and parts more than one mark apart fell from about 13% to 7%. Where the examiner gave partial credit, exact agreement was only 24.6% (Round I) and 32.8% (Round II). Where both gave partial credit, mean absolute difference was 0.92 then 0.72 raw marks. The authors call exact partial-credit scoring the hardest case. Round II's gains came from a revised workflow (page-by-page grading, evidence-location notes, confidence fields, stricter permitted-score checks), and the authors conclude reliable agreement needs a detailed, explicit marking rubric. A rubric rewrite on one 8-mark question, tested only on 72 scripts chosen for large Round I disagreement, cut MAD from 38% to 17% of the part maximum.
claims.quote: [Paraphrase only, to respect the one-quote limit] Locator: Sec. III.3 and Table 4 (7058 parts; 63% to 70% exact; partial-credit parts 24.6% to 32.8%); Sec. V.1 (OE1 Q2 subset, n=72, MAD 38% to 17%).

claims.claim: The AI's own confidence and review flags help triage but cannot justify auto-accepting marks. In Round II, high-confidence parts had much lower mean absolute difference than medium or low-confidence parts: 6.0% vs 17.0% (Olympiad theory), 9.8% vs 28.2% (quantum mechanics), 5.3% vs 27.1% (selection-camp theory) and 6.9% vs 25.6% (selection-camp experiment). Yet in the 1,898-part selection-camp analysis (1,482 theory, 416 experiment parts), accepting every high-confidence, unflagged part would have accepted 1,724 parts, and 87 of them (about 5%) were still more than one mark from the official score. The flags were the model's self-report, with no separately trained routing model tested. The authors conclude the AI belongs in a second-opinion or audit role under examiner control, not as the final marker.
claims.quote: [Paraphrase only, to respect the one-quote limit] Locator: Sec. V.2 and Fig. 12 (MAD by confidence level; 1724 accepted, 87 off by more than 1 mark); Sec. VI conclusion on AI as audit or second-reader tool.

claims.claim: This paper cannot be used to size cost or pick a cheap, Chinese or Indic-capable model. It tested only OpenAI GPT-5.5 (Thinking high for all grading; Pro modes only on the selection camp, one pilot on six scripts). Browser and API runs were mixed, so token counts and run times were not fully logged, and there is no price, latency or throughput figure. The only workload context is human: about 20 graders for about 2.5 days for 350 Olympiad scripts, and about 25 people over four days for the selection camp. Pages were scanned by the exam organisers' team, so no student phone-photo condition was tested. A keyword search of the HTML full text finds no Hindi, Bengali, Assamese, Devanagari or other Indic-script mention, and no mention of data-protection law (scripts were anonymized before AI grading; raw scripts withheld for student privacy). It gives no evidence on non-Latin handwriting accuracy, DPDP compliance or per-paper cost.
claims.quote: [Paraphrase only, to respect the one-quote limit] Locator: Sec. VI (token and time logging gap; human grading workload figures); Table 2 (models and effort settings); Acknowledgments (scan team); Data and materials statement.

results.title: Bodhan AI / AI4Bharat IndicOCR (open-weight Indic document + handwriting OCR) - Hugging Face model card
results.snippet: Only source found with per-language HANDWRITING word accuracy for Assamese/Bengali/Hindi (vendor-reported, Sept 2026; 100x(1-WER)): Gemini 3.1 Pro 71.6/74.8/83.1 (overall 72.0); open-weight IndicOCR 66.1/71.3/77.6 (66.7); Sarvam Vision 47.8/58.3/72.3 (55.4); Gemma-4-31B 24.1/35.1/70.7; Chandra OCR 2 8.9/6.6/54.6; Surya OCR 2 17.8/10.0/42.7. So even the best system misses roughly 17-28% of handwritten words, so human review is needed. Model is 0.8B Qwen3.5-based plus a 33M PP-DocLayoutV3 layout model, handwriting for English + 12 Indian languages incl. Assamese, maths output as LaTeX (card shows handwritten Hindi maths), about 6.3 pages/s on one H100. Indic Open Model License: free commercial self-hosting and fine-tuning; hosting it as an API for others needs written sign-off; bars automated decisions on legal rights without human oversight. Hosted API reported at Rs 0.20/image by Analytics Vidhya (not verified on Bodhan's own page).

results.title: Sarvam Vision 2.1: Pushing the Pareto frontier of document intelligence (24 Sep 2026)
results.snippet: Latest head-to-head of 13 OCR systems on Sarvam Indic OCR Bench v2 (6,909 samples, 22 languages; vendor-run, printed text only, no handwriting; dataset is Apache-2.0 on Hugging Face). Overall: Sarvam Vision 2.1 87.4, Bodhan Indic-OCR 84.9, Gemini 3.6 Flash 79.4, Google Cloud Vision 71.8, Surya OCR 2 70.0, Mistral OCR4 69.2, Azure Vision 4.0 41.3, AWS Textract 4.6. Assamese/Bengali/Hindi: Gemini 3.6 Flash 87.6/90.4/92.1; Google Cloud Vision 86.6/85.2/84.3; Mistral OCR4 86.0/85.1/85.9; Azure 0.2/8.2/85.7 and Textract about 0/7.6/9.7, so Azure and Textract are unusable for Bengali and Assamese. The English OmniDocBench v1.6 table also ranks Chinese open models (PaddleOCR-VL 1.6 96.0, GLM-OCR 94.7, DeepSeek-OCR2 87.9). Announces Indic handwriting recognition without numbers. Sarvam price list (docs.sarvam.ai/api/pricing): Rs 0.5/page digitise, Rs 1/page extract, max 10 pages per job.

results.title: Google Cloud Document AI - processor language support (Enterprise Document OCR handwriting list)
results.snippet: Primary vendor page, read on 8 Oct 2026: Enterprise Document OCR marks handwriting as supported for Hindi, Bengali, Marathi and Nepali (plus English, Arabic, Chinese, Japanese, Korean) but not Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Gujarati or Punjabi; Assamese is not listed at all. Price page (cloud.google.com/document-ai/pricing): $1.50 per 1,000 pages (first 1,000/month free, $0.60 above 5M, optional OCR add-ons $6/1,000), about $0.018 for a 12-page sheet. Contrast from the vendors' own pages: Azure Document Intelligence Read handwriting covers only 12 languages with no Indic script, and AWS Textract handwriting is English-only. No independent handwriting accuracy number for Google on Indic scripts was found.

results.title: OmniHandwritingOCR: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal LLMs in Handwritten OCR Scenarios (arXiv, 19 Aug 2026)
results.snippet: Independent academic benchmark (ECNU, CIKM 2026): 77.57K handwritten images including newly collected student writing and multi-line handwritten maths, 13 systems (7 general MLLMs, 6 OCR models). English and Chinese only, no Indic scripts. Overall CER: Qwen3-VL-8B 30.9% (best), InternVL3-78B 32.2, Qwen2.5-VL-72B 38.9, GPT-4o 48.5, versus OCR specialists PaddleOCR-VL 71.1, DeepSeek-OCR 73.8, GOT-OCR2 84.2, MinerU2.5 125.6. English handwriting CER: Qwen3-VL-8B 16.4, DeepSeek-OCR 39.8, PaddleOCR-VL 47.5. Hard multi-line handwritten formulas: best CER still about 55%. Authors report models hallucinate plausible but visually unsupported corrections. Takeaway: OmniDocBench leaders are weak on handwriting; a general Chinese VLM (Qwen3-VL) is the better open reader.

results.title: WildHandBench: A Benchmark for Handwritten Text Understanding that Challenges MLLMs and Humans (arXiv, 24 Aug 2026)
results.snippet: Independent benchmark of 500 wild handwritten documents (free text, tables, formulas) across 18 models plus a human baseline of 77.09. Gemini 3.1 Pro 71.85, Gemini 3.5 Flash 68.25, Kimi-K3 67.81, Qwen3.5-Plus 65.55, Qwen3-VL-235B 62.19, Claude Opus 4.8 57.70; compact OCR models trail: PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 54.21, GLM-OCR 54.06, dots.ocr 43.73, DeepSeek-OCR2 9.46 (collapses on handwriting). 63-91% of model errors are 'prior-driven', meaning fluent text not supported by the image, versus 49% for humans: a silent-hallucination risk for grading. Chinese and English documents only, no Indic scripts.

results.title: BanglaWild: In-the-Wild Bengali Scene Text Recognition Benchmark for OCR and Vision-Language Models (arXiv, 4 Aug 2026)
results.snippet: Independent test on 2,535 photographed Bengali images (scene text, not handwriting) of 15 VLMs and 3 classic OCRs; the only study found comparing Chinese open VLMs with Western models on Bengali script. CER: Gemini 2.5 Flash 14.1 (best), Alibaba Qwen3.5-9B 20.4 (best open model, level with Gemini 2.5 Pro at 21.7-24.9; larger Qwen3.5 27B/35B slightly worse), Llama 4 Maverick 37, GPT-5.4-mini 53, Gemma-3-12B 64; Claude Haiku 4.5 about 80-90 and InternVL3.5 above 100 fail; Tesseract 98, EasyOCR 48, Surya 191. LoRA fine-tuning rescues weak models (Gemma-3-12B 64 to 29, InternVL3.5-8B 116 to 46) but does not beat zero-shot Qwen3.5-9B. Useful evidence for adding a new script by fine-tuning.

claims.claim: Pervasive hidden transcription errors. In the EDU-CIRCUIT-HW observation set (513 expert-transcribed handwritten university circuit-analysis solutions from 11 students), all six multimodal LLMs used as handwriting transcribers made at least one error in a large share of solutions. Sample error rate was 37.62% for the best (Gemini-3-Pro-Preview), then 53.52% Gemini-2.5-Pro, 61.72% Qwen3-VL-Plus, 71.54% GPT-5.1, 80.70% Claude-4.5-Sonnet and 85.43% for the open-weight Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking (0.61 to 2.79 errors per solution on average). Errors were located by a Gemini-2.5-Pro judge validated against expert annotation (item-level F1 about 0.91, sample-level accuracy 0.96). The authors conclude current MLLMs are not reliable enough for unsupervised high-stakes auto-grading.
claims.quote: "an astonishing scale of latent failures within MLLM-recognized student handwritten content" (Sun et al., arXiv:2602.00095v3, abstract)

claims.claim: Chinese versus Western vision models as transcribers. Alibaba's commercial Qwen3-VL-Plus transcribed handwritten STEM work more accurately than GPT-5.1 and Claude-4.5-Sonnet, but less accurately than Gemini-3-Pro-Preview and Gemini-2.5-Pro. Sample error rate was 61.72% vs 71.54% (GPT-5.1) vs 80.70% (Claude-4.5-Sonnet). Downstream binary/type/point agreement with expert deductions was 80.90/68.62/65.11 vs 77.78/65.50/61.99 vs 77.58/63.16/59.84, with every transcript graded by the same GPT-5.1 grader. The small open-weight Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking was weakest overall (sample error rate 85.43%, point agreement 56.92%) yet made fewer diagram-interpretation errors (98) than Gemini-2.5-Pro (103). No other Chinese model (DeepSeek-OCR, PaddleOCR-VL, GLM-4.xV, InternVL, MinerU, dots.ocr, GOT-OCR), no commercial OCR API and no Indic system was tested.
claims.quote: NO VERBATIM QUOTE (one-quote limit). Evidence locator: Table 5 (observation set) rows Qwen3-VL-Plus, GPT-5.1, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking; Section 4.1 (models and grader used); Section 4.2 and Figure 4 (diagram errors 98 vs 103); Appendix D.4 (API settings).

claims.claim: Fine-grained marking is where LLM grading trails a human marker, and misreads widen the gap. Even given perfect expert transcriptions, the GPT-5.1 grader agreed with expert score deductions at 89.47% (binary: any mistake present or not), 78.36% (same error types) and only 74.46% (exact point deductions), against 83.63% / 82.46% / 81.29% for a human graduate TA grading from the handwriting itself, so the LLM beats the TA only at coarse correctness. Moving from the best recognizer (Gemini-3-Pro-Preview) to the worst (Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking) costs 12.86 points of binary agreement but 17.16 (type) and 17.35 (point). Only 7.60% to 19.60% of individual misreads changed a grade, which is why they hide under coarse marking; character and symbol misreads have the highest grade impact (about 20%) versus often below 10% for diagram and reasoning-text errors.
claims.quote: NO VERBATIM QUOTE (one-quote limit). Evidence locator: Table 5 rows Graduate, Human Expert, Gemini-3-Preview, Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking; Section 4.1 (metric definitions: binary, type, point agreement; error impact rate); Section 4.2 (12.86 / 17.16 / 17.35 point gaps; error impact by category).

claims.claim: A confidence-based routing design recovered most of the accuracy lost to misreads with a small human load. On the 821-solution test set (18 students), a GPT-5.1 detector flagged likely transcription errors using patterns distilled from the observation set. Solutions with uncertain flags went to a human TA (3.3% of solutions when Gemini-2.5-Pro transcribed, 4.4% when GPT-5.1 did) and a further 20.6% / 25.1% were re-graded by an LLM. Exact-point agreement rose from 69.91% to 74.42% (Gemini-2.5-Pro) and from 66.87% to 75.76% (GPT-5.1); binary agreement rose from 85.02% to 86.48% and from 82.34% to 86.60%. Only solutions that already carried deductions were re-examined, because misreads mostly cause wrongful deductions rather than undeserved credit. The abstract's 3.3% therefore describes the Gemini-2.5-Pro setup only, and the resulting 74-76% point agreement is comparable to the expert-transcription oracle (74.46%, measured on the other subset), not better than it.
claims.quote: NO VERBATIM QUOTE (one-quote limit). Evidence locator: Table 6 and Section 5 (Case Study); Appendix D.3 (regrading module; solutions with uncertain error flags referred to the human TA); abstract for the 3.3% headline figure.

claims.claim: Transfer limits for ExamLeaf. The data are 1,334 solutions from 29 students in one US undergraduate circuit-analysis course (62 textbook problems, Spring 2025), scored by doctoral experts on a five-category deduction rubric. Only a two-stage pipeline (MLLM transcription, then GPT-5.1 text grading at high reasoning effort) and a human TA were evaluated, one run per model (temperature 0, except GPT-5.1 fixed at 1). The paper tests no Indic or other non-Latin scripts, does not examine image-capture conditions such as phone photos, and covers no school-level (K-12) work (K-12 benchmarks appear only as prior work). It ran no head-to-head of single-step image grading versus transcribe-then-grade; it only asserts, citing earlier studies, that end-to-end grading from the image is opaque and less reliable at present. The authors warn the findings may not generalize beyond circuit-style diagrams and that any deployment needs human verification.
claims.quote: NO VERBATIM QUOTE (one-quote limit). Evidence locator: Section 2.1 and Table 1 (dataset); Section 4.1, Appendix D.2 and D.4 (pipeline and settings); Section 8 Limitations; Section 9 Ethics (reliability risks); Appendix A.3 (end-to-end grading remark). Source: arXiv v3 dated 30 Apr 2026, Findings of ACL 2026 (Georgia Tech / Virginia Tech).

claims.claim: Handwriting OCR error carries straight into grading in a two-stage pipeline. In the paper's pipeline GPT-4o transcribes the answer sheet and a text-only LLM then grades each question against the key and rubric (no direct image-to-grade condition is reported). Swapping teacher transcriptions for GPT-4o OCR raised grading MAE on a 0-100 scale (Table 1). Total score went from 7.9 to 11.7 (English, GPT-4o grader) and from 6.8 to 11.9 (English, DeepSeek-Chat 671B), and from 1.5 to 8.2 and from 0.8 to 8.1 in Math. Math short-answer MAE rose from 2.9 to 16.3 (GPT-4o) and from 5.9 to 22.8 (DeepSeek). String-matched MCQ score error went from 0.0 to 2.8 (English) and 2.3 (Math) for every grader, so it is purely OCR-caused.
claims.quote: Aisyah et al., arXiv:2506.04822v3, abstract: "the VLM struggles with handwriting recognition, causing error propagation in LLM grading"

claims.claim: The Chinese open-weight DeepSeek-Chat (671B, cited as the DeepSeek-V3 report) was competitive with GPT-4o as a grader, and Qwen2.5-72B and Llama-3.1-70B trailed. With teacher-transcribed input, DeepSeek was best on English (MAE short 4.4, essay 1.5, total 6.8 vs GPT-4o 9.2, 2.7, 7.9). GPT-4o was best on Math components (short 2.9, essay 5.7 vs DeepSeek 5.9, 8.5), though DeepSeek had the lower Math total (0.8 vs 1.5). Qwen2.5-72B totals were 9.2 (English) and 3.3 (Math); Llama-3.1-70B totals were 11.6 and 10.3, with Llama Math essay MAE 19.1. With GPT-4o OCR input, DeepSeek and GPT-4o were level on totals (English 11.9 vs 11.7; Math 8.1 vs 8.2). Llama had the lowest Math total (2.2) despite the worst Math essay error (27.5), so total-score MAE can hide per-question errors; other per-question outliers were Qwen English essay 16.6 and DeepSeek Math short answer 22.8. The Introduction's statement that GPT-4o with vision input achieves the highest accuracy is not what Table 1 shows with teacher transcription.
claims.quote: [locator, no verbatim quote per copyright limit] Table 1 (rows OCR by GPT4o and OCR by Human, Total and component columns); Section 5 Main Result, which names DeepSeek-Chat and GPT-4o as top performers with human transcription; Section 6 Conclusion.

claims.claim: The paper's only OCR-quality numbers are GPT-4o's agreement with teacher transcriptions (Table 4, all schools). Exact match was 65.3% for English short answers vs 24.9% for Math short answers, and 78.5% vs 62.4% for MCQ answers. Essay ROUGE-L was 60.2 (English) vs 22.3 (Math). Handwriting transcription was therefore markedly worse for Math than English. No CER or WER is reported. The metrics are strict string or overlap proxies (Math MCQ exact match is 62.4% although OCR-induced MCQ score MAE is only 2.3), so they likely overstate scoring-relevant errors. GPT-4o was the only OCR model with reported results; Qwen-VL-72B (version unspecified) was tried and judged suboptimal, with no figures given. Data are Latin-script Indonesian/English answers from Grade-4 pupils (no Indic scripts, equations or diagrams).
claims.quote: [locator, no verbatim quote per copyright limit] Table 4 (All rows) and Section 5 OCR Performance Analysis; Section 4 Model paragraph for the Qwen-VL-72B remark; Table 1 MCQ columns.

claims.claim: Even with teacher-transcribed answers (no OCR error), LLM grader error on English answers was roughly 10 to 50 times higher for rural than urban pupils (English is a foreign language for these pupils). Total-score MAE, urban vs rural, was GPT-4o 0.8 vs 23.1, Llama-3.1-70B 2.7 vs 26.9, Qwen2.5-72B 0.5 vs 24.3 and DeepSeek 1.5 vs 21.2 (Table 3; 414 urban and 232 rural answer sheets). Math MAE was similar or lower for rural pupils (e.g. GPT-4o 2.4 urban vs 0.3 rural). The authors suggest, but do not test, that writing style and grammar may explain the gap. This is a group-dependent grader-error pattern.
claims.quote: [locator, no verbatim quote per copyright limit] Table 3 (Urban and Rural blocks) and Section 5 Urban vs. Rural Performance Analysis; sheet counts in Section 3 Data Collection.

claims.claim: In teacher ratings of the generated feedback (two raters, 1-5 scale, below 3 counted as poor, Spearman agreement 0.4-0.7; Indonesian feedback written on top of GPT-4o's grades), DeepSeek-Chat beat GPT-4o in English on clarity (4.04 vs 3.64) and helpfulness (3.96 vs 3.60). In Math, DeepSeek scored only 2.96 on personalization and 2.92 on helpfulness against GPT-4o's 3.72 and 3.68, despite equal or higher clarity (4.00 vs 3.92) and correctness (3.88 vs 3.84). The Conclusion's statement that DeepSeek gives more contextually relevant feedback therefore holds for English only.
claims.quote: [locator, no verbatim quote per copyright limit] Table 2 and Section 5 Human Evaluation on Personalised Feedback; Section 6 Conclusion.

result.publishDate: 2025-06-05 (arXiv v1); numbers read from v3 dated 2026-04-01; accepted at AIED 2026 per arXiv comment

claims.claim: Zhou, Resck, Hui and Korhonen (Language Technology Lab, University of Cambridge; arXiv 2607.14480v3, CC BY 4.0) find that eight multilingual evaluators give semantically identical instruction-response pairs different absolute scores depending on the language. The eight are 4 prompted LLM judges (Aya Expanse 32B, Qwen2.5-72B, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, M-Prometheus-14B) and 4 reward models. The language effect is significant for every evaluator (one-way ANOVA, p<0.001). For the prompted judges the shift is about 0.4-0.5 points on a 1-5 scale. Lower-resource languages, measured by Common Crawl web share, are scored more leniently: for reward models Spearman rho = -0.81 and Pearson r = -0.58, with a weaker association for prompted judges. Scope caveat: the data are RewardBench and M-RewardBench chat, safety, math and code prompts (the rejected responses were scored), not exam answers marked against a rubric.
claims.quote: multilingual evaluators assign significantly different scores to different evaluation languages

claims.claim: Hindi (Devanagari) is the only Indian language among the 23 tested and is consistently among the most leniently scored. English, Italian, French and Spanish sit at the strict end, and English has the lowest normalised score for reward models. Assamese and Bengali are not in the set (Table 3: ar, cs, de, el, en, es, fa, fr, he, hi, id, it, ja, ko, nl, pl, pt, ro, ru, tr, uk, vi, zh), so any leniency for them is an extrapolation, not a measurement in this paper.
claims.quote: Hindi, Hebrew, and Arabic appear in the top quartile of language scores

claims.claim: Two frontier judges reproduce the bias on the Safety and Chat-Hard splits over all 23 languages (Table 1, section 3.5). GPT-4.1-mini: per-language score range 0.63 and 0.55 points on the 1-5 scale, global-threshold acceptance-rate gaps 19.6 and 14.0 pp. Qwen3-32B in thinking mode: range 1.28 and 0.71 points, gaps 32.7 and 29.7 pp, so the Chinese open-weight model showed the larger spread in this test. Resource-level Spearman rho is between -0.58 and -0.73 (all p<0.01), and Hindi is among the three most lenient languages in all four settings. Gemini, Claude and DeepSeek judges were not tested.
claims.quote: Both reproduce the pattern

claims.claim: High pairwise accuracy does not reveal the language bias. Evaluators reach above 90% pairwise accuracy (often 90-95%+), yet reward models differ by up to 43 percentage points in acceptance rate across languages under one global 50th-percentile threshold, and by up to 34 pp even where pairwise accuracy exceeds 95%. Example: Skywork-LLaMA-8B had 93% pairwise accuracy and 23% acceptance in English versus 87% and 67% in Ukrainian. Inference for ExamLeaf, not tested on exams: validating an AI marker only by ranking agreement with teachers could hide language-specific inflation of absolute marks.
claims.quote: above 90% pairwise accuracy, yet have up to 43% difference in acceptance rate

claims.claim: Calibration helps but is not a full fix. A per-language additive offset, equivalent to language-specific thresholds, cut the cross-language acceptance-rate gap by 60.9% on average (33.4 to 11.6 pp, reward models, Appendix D, Table 13). A residual gap remains because 18.8% of centred-score variance is language-by-item interaction and score spread differs by language. Per-language thresholds also need language identification, which code-switching defeats: langdetect labelled 44% of English-wrapped Hindi safety prompts as English, and acceptance rose from the calibrated 50% to 75% (Skywork-LLaMA-8B). Inference for ExamLeaf: science answers that mix Assamese, Bengali or Hindi with English terms are naturally code-switched.
claims.quote: Per-language thresholds would require language identification, which can be defeated by code-switched prompts

results.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 (G.S.R. 846(E), 13 Nov 2025): full notified text
results.snippet: Verbatim Gazette text, read in full. The official MeitY copy (meity.gov.in/static/uploads/2025/11/53450e6e5dc0bfa85ebd78686cadad39.pdf) returns 403 to bots, so this mirror was used. Rule 1(4): the main duties (Rules 3, 5-16) start 18 months after publication, about 13 May 2027. Rule 10: verifiable parental consent before processing any child's (under 18) data, with the parent checked against held ID/age records or a government or DigiLocker token. Rule 12 + Fourth Schedule Part A(3): the 'educational institution' carve-out only lifts the tracking and behavioural-monitoring ban for educational activities or safety. It is not a general consent waiver, and whether a private edtech counts as an 'educational institution' is arguable (PIB's plain-language note that education is exempt overstates it). Rule 15: transfer abroad is allowed by default, subject to any Central Government requirements about foreign states or entities they control; commentary (Mondaq, 26 Mar 2026) says no country had been restricted. Rule 6: encryption, access control, logs kept 1 year, processor contracts. Rule 7: breach report to the Board within 72 hours. Rule 13: Significant Data Fiduciaries need annual DPIA/audit and algorithmic due diligence. PIB explainer (17 Nov 2025): penalties up to Rs 200 crore for children's-data failures, Rs 250 crore for security failures. Act s.8(3), checked separately on dpdpa.com, requires accuracy of data used for decisions affecting a person, which bears on AI-awarded marks. LiveLaw (1 Aug 2026): the Data Protection Board still had no chair or members.

results.title: 2026 CBSE On-Screen Marking controversy (Wikipedia)
results.snippet: Best single timeline of India's largest digitised-marking failure. CBSE Class 12 (results 13 May 2026) scanned about 98.7 lakh answer books through vendor Coempt Eduteck (reported to be formerly Globarena). Reported faults: blurred scans, missing pages, other students' scripts, unmarked answers, unexpectedly low marks. Pass rate fell from 88.39% to 85.2%; about 4.04 lakh students asked for scanned copies; chairman and secretary were removed on 2 Jun 2026 and procurement was probed. Corroborating news: NSUI PIL in Delhi High Court (notice 8 Jun 2026); Delhi GSTA teachers' body said OSM was rolled out without training or testing and caused over-cautious, stricter marking (National Herald, 29 May 2026); CBSE categorically denied any AI marking, saying human teachers only (Tribune, 13 Feb 2026). Lessons: boards are politically sensitive about anything resembling AI marking; scan/photo quality and script mix-ups dominate failures; and Globarena's 2019 Telangana inter-results fiasco (about 20 reported student suicides) shows the stakes of result errors. Wikipedia is a tertiary summary, so check the cited news. No AI was involved in OSM itself.

results.title: Evaluating AI Grading on Real-World Handwritten College Mathematics: A Large-Scale Study Toward a Benchmark (UC Irvine, Mar 2026)
results.snippet: A real OCR + LLM grader on thousands of handwritten calculus quiz submissions from nearly 800 students; AI marks were 'for reference only' and TAs stayed the official graders. OCR: GPT-4.1-mini transcribed 84% acceptably versus 55% for Mathpix on a hard 171-solution subset (about 88% across all scripts). Grading: mean absolute gap to TAs 0.5-1.06 points per quiz, 68-86% within 1 point. Independent review of 3,851 records found 79.8% of AI evaluations fully correct, 9.6% acceptable, 10.7% incorrect. Failure modes: diagrams and geometry, crossed-out work, nested fractions, hallucinated solutions in blank boxes, silent 'autocorrection' of student mistakes (under 2%), over-penalising valid methods missing from the rubric, and leniency to rubric-shaped but wrong reasoning. Authors admit they have no systematic rule for when to defer to a human and say high-stakes use needs far stricter human-in-the-loop controls. English and maths only, low-stakes quizzes, no Indic scripts.

results.title: Vision-Language Models for Criterion-Level Grading of Handwritten Examinations in Outcome-Based Education (IEEE TLT / arXiv, Sep 2026)
results.snippet: Direct page-image grading, no separate OCR step. 1,982 criterion-level marks from 485 handwritten English university answers (nine subjects, with equations and diagrams); 20 configurations of Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, Pixtral and Donut. Chinese open-weight Qwen2.5-VL-7B with LoRA reached QWK 0.727 and MAE 0.435 marks against the examiner, above the mean human-to-human QWK of 0.551. That reflects calibration to one examiner's marks, and few-shot prompting lowered QWK for every model. Key warning: ICC was 0.79-0.87, yet 50-64% of criteria changed marks across five sampled runs, so use greedy (temperature 0) decoding and keep criterion-level records. Errors concentrate in high-weight and code or diagram criteria, which should go to teacher review. Limits: one institution, one examiner's labels, no comparison with an OCR-plus-text-grader pipeline, no Indic scripts.

results.title: Handbook on Data Protection and Privacy for Developers of AI in India (Ikigai Law with GIZ FAIR Forward, DSCI, NASSCOM; Jan 2026)
results.snippet: Practitioner guide to the DPDP Act and Rules for Indian AI builders (guidance, not law). Relevant points: the fiduciary stays liable for its processors and needs a written contract; a model provider reached by API that also decides logging or fine-tuning can become a joint data fiduciary (worked example), so zero-retention and no-training terms matter when routing student images through aggregators or foreign APIs. Children's data needs verifiable parental consent plus age-gating, and data collected for one purpose cannot later train models without fresh consent. Tracking or behavioural monitoring of children is barred outside the Fourth Schedule cases even with parental consent. Cross-border transfer is allowed unless the government notifies restrictions; Significant Data Fiduciaries face audits, DPIAs and algorithmic due diligence.

results.title: Eklavvya: AI Answer Sheet Checking (Indian vendor view, with pilots and price points from other Indian products)
results.snippet: All vendor self-reported. Eklavvya, an established Indian on-screen-marking vendor with university clients and CERT-In/ISO 27001 claims, treats AI as a 'draft scorer' (its help page): examiners calibrate on a 20-25% sample, AI grades the rest, flagged or borderline answers go to faculty, with accept/override/comment audit trail and four strictness modes. Languages listed: English, Hindi, Marathi, Tamil, Telugu; Assamese is not mentioned. Its '~95% agreement, 85-90% on descriptive answers' cites an unnamed '2025 study'; the same unsourced figure appears on other vendor pages, so treat it as marketing. Other pages checked: E-Valuate AI is the only one with published prices (Rs 2 per page, minimum Rs 8-10 per sheet; annual plans Rs 24,000-60,000; English only; 48-hour auto-delete). Chanakya AI claims 95% OCR accuracy and 3-5 marks variance from a 250-sheet Delhi-NCR pilot; Saraswati AI (Hindi/English) and Smartail DeepGrade (Andhra expansion, Jul 2026) publish no accuracy numbers. None makes a specific DPDP or data-residency commitment. Gradescope's AI grading is Institutional-tier only; aggregator sites quote about $1-5 per student per course (unverified). State pilots: Jodhpur graded 70,000 students' answers in 3 days (Elets, Apr 2026) and Maharashtra piloted 'AI-assisted' on-screen evaluation in the Jun-Jul 2026 supplementary exams, both with no accuracy data.

claims.claim: OpenRouter's data_collection setting defaults to 'allow', which permits routing to providers that store user data non-transiently and may train on it. Setting it to 'deny' (per request, or account-wide in privacy settings) restricts routing to providers that do not collect user data. Children's exam-sheet images sent with default settings can therefore reach storing or training providers.
claims.quote: (default) allow providers which store user data non-transiently and may train on it

claims.claim: Setting the per-request `zdr` flag to true restricts routing to endpoints that have a Zero Data Retention policy. ZDR can also be enforced account-wide, per model group, or through guardrails. The per-request flag acts as an OR with those settings, so it can only add enforcement and never relax an account-wide setting.
claims.quote: the request will only be routed to endpoints that have a Zero Data Retention policy

claims.claim: Providers can be restricted per request with `only` (allow-list), `ignore` (block-list) and `order`, alongside `allow_fallbacks` (default true). An account-wide allowed-providers setting acts as a ceiling, and the request fails with a 404 if no provider satisfies both that list and the request's `only` list. The docs warn that allowing only some providers may significantly reduce fallback options and limit request recovery, which is a reliability trade-off for exam-season peaks.
claims.quote: If no provider satisfies both, the request fails with a 404.

claims.claim: OpenRouter's documented regional data residency is limited to the EU and the US. In-region routing works by sending requests to eu.openrouter.ai or us.openrouter.ai and is available only on the Business and Enterprise plans. The page names no India or other Asian region (no mention of India, Asia or Mumbai anywhere on it).
claims.quote: OpenRouter supports in-region routing in the EU and US on the Business and Enterprise plans.

claims.claim: OpenRouter states that the Data Policy tags it shows on model pages for providers that may log prompts are best-effort. They are not a definitive record of third-party providers' data policies.
claims.quote: This is not a definitive source of third party data policies, but represents our best knowledge.

results.title: IndicOCR (bodhan-ai/indic-ocr) model card - Bodhan AI and AI4Bharat, Hugging Face, Sep 2026
results.snippet: Open-weight (gated, auto-approved; Indic Open Model License v1.0). Two stages: 33M layout model with exam-style labels (Question, Answer, Equation, Diagram, MCQ) plus a Qwen3.5-0.8B recogniser. Handwriting supported for English + 12 languages incl. Assamese, Bengali, Hindi. Vendor-run IndicOCR-HW table, word accuracy (Assamese/Bengali/Hindi): Gemini 3.1 Pro 71.6/74.8/83.1, IndicOCR 66.1/71.3/77.6, Sarvam Vision 47.8/58.3/72.3, Surya OCR 2 17.8/10.0/42.7, Chandra OCR 2 8.9/6.6/54.6, i.e. 17-28% word errors even for the best system; test set not described. About 6.3 pages/s on one H100 (English OmniDocBench pages). Licence: commercial use and fine-tuning allowed, derivatives keep the licence, running it as a hosted API for third parties needs Bodhan's written sign-off, no automated decisions on legal rights without human oversight. Hosted API Rs 0.20/image (Analytics Vidhya, 10 Sep 2026). Same release: Indic-Translate (22 languages incl. Assamese) and Indic-Speak TTS (Assamese included).

results.title: IndicPage-OCR: Robust Low-Resource Adaptation for Multi-Script Indic Handwritten Page Recognition (IIIT Hyderabad, DAS 2026)
results.snippet: Recipe and cost for adding a script. LoRA (rank 8) on the 0.5B Qwen decoder of GOT-OCR 2.0, vision encoder frozen, one adapter per language, one 48 GB RTX 6000 Ada, about 200K steps at batch 4; data per language 5.5K-23.9K real pages (Bengali 7,189) plus about 12M augmented word/line samples in total. Word-to-line-to-page curriculum is essential (page-only WER 0.44-0.61 vs 0.04-0.08). Page-level handwritten Bengali WER/CER: Sarvam 0.054/0.019, Gemini Flash 0.058/0.021, IndicPage-OCR 0.072/0.022; zero-shot Qwen2.5-VL-3B 2.7/3.9, DeepSeek-OCR 7.0/8.0 (runaway output), Chandra 0.36/0.12, Tesseract 0.96/0.81. Hindi: 0.068, 0.071, 0.082 vs DeepSeek-OCR 4.2. 12.4 s/page. Caveats: authors' in-house pages (500 per language), no Assamese, and the same systems score far worse on Bodhan's handwriting set, so test on real student scripts. LoRA adapters for Bengali/Hindi/Tamil/Telugu on Hugging Face (SHAON123). Precursor HindiOCR-VLM (ICDAR 2025) reached only WRR 36.7 on printed Marathi, same script, without Marathi training.

results.title: Unconstrained Camera Captured Indic Offline Handwritten Dataset (IIIT-Indic-HW-UC), IIIT Hyderabad, ICPR 2024
results.snippet: Phone-photographed handwriting, the closest public match to ExamLeaf's input: 91K A4 pages, 13 languages incl. Assamese (80 writers, 200K word crops, 53K unique words) and Bengali (158 writers), 1,220 writers in all, page-level JSON with boxes, reading order and transcripts. Free per-language zips (Assamese 4.3 GB, Bengali 7.9 GB, Hindi 3.6 GB); no licence stated, so confirm commercial use with IIIT-H. Baseline CNN-BLSTM-CTC word-level accuracy on camera pages (CRR/WRR): Assamese 90.98/85.15, Bengali 96.60/89.10, Hindi 93.88/84.69. A Bengali model trained on flatbed scans falls from WRR 84.3 to 51.5 on camera pages. IIIT-INDIC-HW-WORDS, PLATTER/CHIPS (IIT Bombay, arXiv 2502.06172) and the ICDAR 2025 IHDR data omit Assamese; the only other Assamese set is OAHTD (ICON 2024: 410 pages, 300 writers aged 10-76, IEEE DataPort subscription).

results.title: Sarvam Vision 2.1: Pushing the Pareto frontier of document intelligence (Sarvam AI, 24 Sep 2026)
results.snippet: Commercial Indic document API covering Assamese. Sarvam Indic OCR Bench (6,909 printed/historical blocks, Apache-2.0 on Hugging Face; not handwriting), accuracy Assamese/Bengali/Hindi: Sarvam Vision 2.1 90.9/93.5/93.5, Bodhan Indic-OCR 89.4/90.9/91.0, Gemini 3.6 Flash 87.6/90.4/92.1, Google Cloud Vision 86.6/85.2/84.3, Surya OCR 2 87.3/81.8/86.1, Mistral OCR4 86.0/85.1/85.9, Azure Vision 4.0 0.2/8.2/85.7, AWS Textract 0.0/7.6/9.7 (Azure and Textract effectively cannot read Assamese or Bengali). Version 2.1 adds Indic handwritten recognition trained on synthetic plus real data but publishes no handwriting error rates. Proprietary weights. Digitisation API Rs 0.50/page, Extraction API Rs 1.00/page on Sarvam's pricing page (12 pages = Rs 6). Vendor-run benchmark.

results.title: BanglaWild: An In-the-Wild Bengali Scene Text Recognition Benchmark for OCR and Vision-Language Models (arXiv, 4 Aug 2026)
results.snippet: Best open comparison of Chinese vs Western models on Bengali-Assamese script, but scene text, not handwriting (1,014 test images). Zero-shot CER/WER, best realistic prompt: Gemini 2.5 Flash 14.1/30.0, Claude Sonnet 4.6 18.5/39.7, Qwen3.5-9B 20.4/45.2, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B 20.2/42.9, Gemini 2.5 Pro 21.7/36.4, Qwen3.5-27B 23.5/47.7, Llama 4 Maverick 37.0/59.4, GPT-5.4-mini 53.4/81.2, Claude Haiku 4.5 82/109, InternVL3.5-8B 116/127 (collapses); EasyOCR 48/89, Tesseract 98/110. LoRA on only 1,268 images rescues weak models (InternVL3.5-8B CER 116 -> 45.8, Gemma-3-12B 63.9 -> 28.9) but barely moves Qwen3.5-9B (CER 20.4 -> 21.5, WER 45.2 -> 40.2): small-data LoRA fixes catastrophic failures, it does not lift strong models.

results.title: When VLMs 'Fix' Students: Identifying and Penalizing Over-Correction in the Evaluation of Multi-line Handwritten Math OCR (ETRI, arXiv, Apr 2026)
results.snippet: Handwritten-maths OCR failure mode that matters for marking (English only). 15 VLMs on FERMAT (2,244 multi-line grade 7-12 handwritten solutions, mostly with planted errors): every model silently corrects the student's mistake in 42-66% of transcriptions (Qwen2.5-VL-32B 66.2%, Llama-3.2-11B 42.1%), and stronger models over-correct more. Gemini 2.5 Flash is the most faithful transcriber (PINK 0.94); GPT-4o is heavily penalised; Qwen2.5-VL-72B/32B, Ovis2-34B and InternVL3-78B follow at 0.91-0.92. A 'transcribe exactly what is written' prompt cuts over-correction only about 4 points on average and lowers scores for the strongest open models. Implication: OCR-then-grade can inflate marks; use a faithful transcriber and send low-confidence lines to teacher review.
