claims.claim: OpenRouter can require Zero Data Retention routing globally (account privacy settings), per model group, per guardrail (fields enforce_zdr_anthropic, _openai, _google, _xai, _other; the older enforce_zdr is deprecated) or per request with `provider: {zdr: true}`. The request flag is OR-combined with the account and guardrail settings, so it can only tighten routing and never loosen a stricter account setting. Turning on the Anthropic, OpenAI or Google group removes only the first-party endpoint: Claude stays reachable via Bedrock and Vertex, GPT via Azure, Gemini via Vertex (AI Studio is dropped). The xAI group (named SpaceXAI on the page) keeps its ZDR endpoint, and the all-other-models group drops every non-ZDR endpoint. The page does not document the error returned when a model has no ZDR endpoint, or how zdr interacts with only/ignore/order/allow_fallbacks.
claims.quote: [no quote; see page sections Per-Request ZDR Enforcement and Per-Model-Group ZDR Enforcement]

claims.claim: OpenRouter's own policy is to keep no prompts unless the account opts in to prompt logging, so under ZDR the retention exposure sits with the upstream endpoint. OpenRouter works with providers to track each endpoint's policy, sometimes through special agreements with stricter terms than the provider default. Where it cannot establish a policy it assumes the endpoint both retains and trains on data, and an endpoint that differs from its provider's default may be unavailable under ZDR-only. Not training is not the same as not retaining: some endpoints do not train but keep data for abuse scanning or legal reasons.
claims.quote: "your prompts are not retained unless you specifically opt in to prompt logging" (OpenRouter docs, Zero Data Retention page)

claims.claim: ZDR in OpenRouter's sense is narrower than nothing being stored anywhere. In-memory implicit prompt caching is deliberately not counted as retention, so cache-enabled endpoints stay eligible; this suits re-sending the same marking scheme with every answer sheet. ZDR covers inference routing only, not plugins or tools such as web search, which may be run by third parties with their own retention. A BYOK key follows the same ZDR rules as OpenRouter credits unless you declare your own zero-retention agreement on the key. For private deployments, a declaration is the customer's attestation: OpenRouter records it and routes on it without independently verifying the upstream's behaviour.
claims.quote: [no quote; see page sections Caching, ZDR with BYOK Keys, ZDR for Private Deployments, and the Warning box near the top]

claims.claim: The ZDR table on the page is rendered live from https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/endpoints/zdr, which on 2026-10-07 listed 942 endpoints, 350 models and 61 providers. Vision-capable Chinese open-weight models eligible under ZDR (listed USD per million input/output tokens): Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Instruct on DeepInfra at $0.20/$0.88 (262,144 context, fp8; also Parasail, Venice, Novita), Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct on DeepInfra at $0.15/$0.60 (also Novita, SiliconFlow), Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct on Parasail only ($0.25/$0.75), GLM-4.6V on Z.AI and Novita at $0.30/$0.90 (131,072 context), and DeepSeek V4 Flash vision-exp on DeepInfra, Novita and SiliconFlow. Western comparators in the same list: Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite $0.10/$0.40 and Gemini 2.5 Flash $0.30/$2.50 via Google Vertex; GPT-5 mini $0.25/$2.00 and GPT-4.1 mini $0.40/$1.60 via Azure only; Claude Haiku 4.5 $1.00/$5.00 via Bedrock and Vertex. ZDR-eligible pools are thin (4, 3 and 1 endpoints for the three Qwen3-VL instruct sizes). The list contains no OCR-specialist model (PaddleOCR, DeepSeek-OCR, GOT-OCR, dots.ocr, MinerU, Mistral OCR) and no Sarvam or other Indic-lab model.
claims.quote: [no quote; data from the page's linked feed https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/endpoints/zdr, retrieved 2026-10-07 19:16 UTC and filtered by model id and provider]

claims.claim: ZDR is a retention filter, not a residency or jurisdiction filter. The page never mentions India, DPDP, GDPR, data residency or jurisdiction. In the live ZDR feed (2026-10-07), none of the 942 endpoints has an Indian region in its name or tag. Regions seen are global, US, EU/Europe, eu-west-1, us-east-1/2, us-west-2, swedencentral, us-central1, us-east5 and us-south1, and many tags carry no region at all. 84 of the 942 endpoints are run by Chinese labs or China-founded hosts (Z.AI 14, Moonshot AI 4, Minimax 7, Tencent 6, Seed/ByteDance 11, SiliconFlow 42). Enabling ZDR alone therefore neither keeps children's handwriting out of Chinese-run endpoints nor offers an India-pinned option; a provider allow-list would be needed, and that is documented elsewhere. Region-pinned variants are listed about 10% above the global/base endpoint (96 of 109 region-versus-base pairs for Google, Bedrock, Azure and Mistral; the remaining 13 equal).
claims.quote: [no quote; absence of India, DPDP, GDPR and residency wording checked across the full page text; counts computed from the page's linked feed]

claims.claim: On the model authors' own IndicOCR-HW handwriting benchmark (word accuracy = 100 x (1 - WER)), handwritten Assamese is read at only 66.1% by the open-weight 0.8B IndicOCR model and 71.6% by Gemini 3.1 Pro, the best system tested. That is word error rates of roughly 34% and 28%. Bengali scores 71.3% (IndicOCR) / 74.8% (Gemini 3.1 Pro), Hindi 77.6% / 83.1%, English 80.7% / 84.4%; overall 66.7% / 72.0%. Printed Assamese is 90.2% for IndicOCR, so handwriting is far harder. Table column order: Gemini 3.1 Pro, IndicOCR, Sarvam Vision, Gemma-4-31B, Chandra OCR 2, Surya OCR 2. The numbers are self-reported by the vendor. The page does not describe the benchmark's size, writers or source documents (not shown to be exam answer sheets), and its Limitations section says handwriting recognition is still being improved. Handwriting is supported for English plus only 12 Indian languages (Assamese, Bengali and Hindi included).

In the same handwriting table, the other systems tested are far behind on Assamese/Bengali/Hindi handwriting. Sarvam Vision scores 47.8 / 58.3 / 72.3 (Assamese / Bengali / Hindi). Surya OCR 2 scores 17.8 / 10.0 / 42.7. Chandra OCR 2 scores 8.9 / 6.6 / 54.6. Gemma-4-31B scores 24.1 / 35.1 / 70.7. Overall handwriting word accuracy: Gemini 3.1 Pro 72.0, IndicOCR 66.7, Sarvam Vision 55.4, Gemma-4-31B 33.9, Chandra OCR 2 24.7, Surya OCR 2 23.0. In this vendor benchmark only a frontier VLM (Gemini 3.1 Pro) and the new IndicOCR are in a plausibly usable range for Assamese/Bengali handwriting. Surya OCR 2 is near-unusable there (10-18% word accuracy).

On the page's English-only benchmarks, Baidu's PaddleOCRVL-1.6 (the only Chinese-lab OCR model on the page) leads OmniDocBench 1.6 with overall 96.36, versus Chandra OCR 2 93.11, IndicOCR 92.76, GPT-5.6-sol 92.46, Gemini 3.1 Pro 91.15. It trails IndicOCR on olmOCR-Bench (78.7 vs 82.2). PaddleOCRVL-1.6 is not in the Indic printed (IndicOCR-PR) or handwriting (IndicOCR-HW) tables, and the page shows no results for DeepSeek-OCR, dots.ocr, MinerU, GOT-OCR, Qwen-VL, GLM or InternVL. It therefore gives no Indic-script (Assamese/Bengali) evidence for the Chinese OCR models, and no commercial OCR API (Google, Azure, Textract, Mistral OCR) is benchmarked either.

Self-hosting data point: the pipeline is a 33M-parameter layout detector (133 MB, fp32) plus a 0.8B-parameter Qwen3.5-0.8B-based OCR model (1.7 GB, bf16), using the Sarvam-30B tokenizer. On one NVIDIA H100 80GB with vLLM it reaches 6.34 pages/s at concurrency 128 (median 9,337 ms, p95 72,970 ms per page), and 5.13 pages/s at concurrency 32 (median 3,295 ms, p95 19,243 ms). Throughput saturates near 6.3 pages/s. Derived arithmetic, not on the page: about 22,800 pages/hour, or about 1,900 twelve-page papers/hour per GPU. It was measured on OmniDocBench V1.6 English-subset documents, not dense Indic handwriting, so Indic-script throughput may differ. The p95 latency tail is long under load.

Licence and access terms matter for a commercial exam checker. The Indic Open Model License v1.0 allows free commercial use, self-hosting and fine-tuning/distilling/quantizing. Derivatives must carry the same licence and the credit line 'Built with [Model Name] from Bodhan AI / AI4Bharat'. Running it as an API or hosted service that other people or companies call directly needs Bodhan AI's written sign-off, unless the user is a nonprofit, government or academic body, or publicly releases an equally capable open version within 90 days. A separate commercial licence is needed only at 500M+ monthly active users or $250M+ annual revenue. The licence bans 'automated decisions that affect someone's legal rights without human oversight'. The page does not say whether an end-user app that calls the model internally counts as a hosted service, so written confirmation is advisable. The weights are gated on Hugging Face (auto-approval form asking company, country and intended use). The repo is new: created 2026-08-07, last modified 2026-09-07, 1,460 downloads and 48 likes at fetch.
claims.quote: that needs Bodhan AI's written sign-off first

claims.claim: Sarvam AI's own blog post (published 2026-09-24; page metadata shows last modified 2026-10-06) says Sarvam Vision 2.1 adds Indic handwritten recognition, and that its Digitize API converts handwritten content for English plus 22 Indic languages, a list that includes Assamese, Bengali and Hindi. Handwriting is shown only through demo videos. The post gives no handwriting-specific error rate or accuracy score, so handwritten Assamese/Bengali/Hindi exam accuracy is unmeasured in this source.
claims.quote: handwritten content across English and 22 Indic languages

claims.claim: On Sarvam's own Indic OCR Bench (accuracy %, listed as Assamese / Bengali / Hindi), Sarvam Vision 2.1 scores 90.88 / 93.47 / 93.52, versus Bodhan Indic-OCR 89.41 / 90.87 / 90.99, Gemini 3.6 Flash 87.55 / 90.36 / 92.11, Opus 5 86.62 / 88.75 / 89.38, Surya OCR 2 87.25 / 81.79 / 86.12, Google Cloud Vision 86.58 / 85.24 / 84.29, Azure Vision 4.0 0.22 / 8.24 / 85.72 and AWS Textract 0.02 / 7.56 / 9.67. Sarvam's lead over Gemini 3.6 Flash in these three target languages is only 3.3 / 3.1 / 1.4 points. The overall gap is larger (87.39 vs 79.35), including extreme cases such as Manipuri (85.12 vs 0.55). Textract and Azure are near zero on Assamese and Bengali, and Textract is also near zero on Hindi.
claims.quote: Data pointer, figures only (no prose quoted): Sarvam Indic OCR Bench language-wise accuracy table, rows Overall accuracy, Assamese, Bengali, Hindi, Manipuri.

claims.claim: The Indic OCR Bench is built and run by Sarvam, not by an independent party, and it is not a student-handwriting test. It has 6,909 samples (6,609 across 22 Indian languages plus 300 English), drawn from newspapers, brochures, textbooks and historical writings dated from 1800 to the present, curated to measure character and word accuracy. Every compared system was evaluated by Sarvam itself under one harness, and no handwritten-subset score is reported. The dataset is hosted on Hugging Face (sarvamai/indic-ocr-bench), so ExamLeaf could re-run it on other OCR systems, but the figures should not be read as handwritten-exam accuracy.
claims.quote: Prose paraphrased, not quoted: section Sarvam Indic OCR Bench (sample counts, source types, 1800 to present, Hugging Face link) and section The Pareto frontier of document intelligence (every point evaluated by Sarvam under one harness).

claims.claim: PaddleOCR-VL 1.6, GLM-OCR and DeepSeek-OCR2 are benchmarked in the post only on the English and structure tests, not on the Indic table, and Qwen-VL, InternVL, MinerU, dots.ocr and GOT-OCR do not appear anywhere on the page. OmniDocBench v1.6 overall: PaddleOCR-VL 1.6 96.01 (ahead of Sarvam Vision 2.1 at 94.97), GLM-OCR 94.71, DeepSeek-OCR2 87.91. olmOCR-Bench overall: Sarvam Vision 2.1 87.3, PaddleOCR-VL 1.6 81.1, GLM-OCR 78.9, DeepSeek-OCR2 78.7. The post therefore gives no Assamese, Bengali or Hindi accuracy figures for these Chinese OCR models.
claims.quote: Data pointer, figures only (no prose quoted): olmOCR-Bench and OmniDocBench v1.6 Overall columns; the Indic OCR Bench table has 13 system columns and none is PaddleOCR-VL, GLM-OCR or DeepSeek-OCR2.

claims.claim: Architecture and commercial terms as stated by Sarvam: a harness-with-VLM design (a semantic layout parser plus a pointer reading-order network around a vision-language model). The VLM can run directly at page or document level but with an accuracy trade-off, which is why the harness is used. Indic handwriting training data mixed synthetic forms with real-world sources including videos, followed by supervised fine-tuning and then RLVR. Access is through the Digitize and Extract APIs and the Akshar Document Agents (human-in-the-loop). The post gives no per-page price (it only says serving is now cheaper than the price announced at the February 2026 launch), no parameter count or open-weights status, and no latency or India data-residency statement.
claims.quote: Prose paraphrased, not quoted: sections Introduction, Data and Model Architecture, and Try out now.

claims.claim: Google Document AI's Enterprise Document OCR processor (API type OCR_PROCESSOR, General Availability) flags handwriting as Supported for Bengali/Bangla (bn, Beng script) and Hindi (hi, Deva), and also for Marathi, Nepali (both Deva) and English. Read from the page's raw HTML: each flag is an icon with aria-label 'Supported', so text-only scrapers show the column blank. The page gives no CER/WER accuracy figures and no per-page prices (only a footer link to pricing), so 'Supported' means offered, not measured.
claims.quote: Bengali | bn | Beng | [Handwriting supported: aria-label="Supported"]; Hindi | hi | Deva | [aria-label="Supported"]

claims.claim: Assamese (BCP 47 'as') is absent from the Enterprise Document OCR language table (60 rows) and from the whole page (zero occurrences of 'Assamese' or 'Assam'); Odia is absent too. This page therefore documents no handwriting support for Assamese, ExamLeaf's first-market language. Bengali (bn, Beng) is the nearest listed entry; Assamese is conventionally coded as Beng script, which is general knowledge, not stated on the page. The description says 200+ languages overall while the table lists only 60, so printed-text Assamese support is not ruled out by this page alone.
claims.quote: Table columns: "Language Name", "BCP 47 Tag", "Script", "Handwriting supported" - no row for Assamese

claims.claim: In the same Enterprise Document OCR table, 12 of 60 rows are flagged handwriting 'Not Supported' (48 are 'Supported'). They include six Indian-language scripts: Gujarati (Gujr), Kannada (Knda), Malayalam (Mlym), Punjabi (Guru), Tamil (Taml) and Telugu (Telu). Among Indic languages, Google therefore documents handwriting only for Bengali and the Devanagari-script languages (Hindi, Marathi, Nepali). The Form Parser table lists only Hindi, Marathi and Nepali among Indic rows, so Bengali is not a documented Form Parser language.
claims.quote: Tamil | ta | Taml | [Handwriting supported: aria-label="Not Supported"]

claims.claim: The Enterprise Document OCR entry lists asia-south1 (Google Cloud's Mumbai region) first among its supported regions, so a processor can be created in an Indian region, which is relevant to DPDP-Act data-residency options. The page says nothing about India, residency guarantees or DPDP, and notes that availability varies by processor version (v2.1.1, Public Preview, is stated as unavailable in US, EU and asia-southeast1).
claims.quote: Supported regions: asia-south1, asia-southeast1, australia-southeast1, eu, europe-west2, europe-west3, northamerica-northeast1, us

claims.claim: Enterprise Document OCR request limits on the page are 15 pages for online/synchronous requests, 500 pages for batch/asynchronous requests, and 30 pages in imageless mode, so a 12-page answer sheet is under the synchronous cap. Listed versions are pretrained-ocr-v2.0-2023-06-02 and v2.1-2024-08-07 (Stable, GA) and v2.1.1-2025-01-31 (release candidate, Public Preview). The page was last updated 2026-10-05.
claims.quote: Maximum pages (online/synchronous requests): 15; (batch/offline/asynchronous requests): 500

claims.claim: In a zero-shot test of 13 systems on 77,572 handwritten images (English text, Chinese text, LaTeX formulas, one identical generic transcription instruction), the 8B Chinese open-weight Qwen3-VL-8B was best overall (pooled 1-NED 75.63, CER 30.94, WER 32.94). It was well ahead of GPT-4o (59.32 / 48.53 / 50.03) and of every dedicated OCR model. The best OCR specialist was Nanonets-OCR2-3B (68.42 / 42.27 / 42.77). The two Chinese OCR-specialist VLMs, DeepSeek-OCR (64.27 / 73.84 / 69.94) and PaddleOCR-VL (62.73 / 71.14 / 72.38), had more than twice Qwen3-VL-8B's CER on handwriting. Scope limit: English, Chinese and maths only, no Indic scripts.
claims.quote: Table 4 (pooled; 1-NED / CER / WER, %): Qwen3-VL-8B 75.63/30.94/32.94; Kimi-VL-A3B 73.58/38.20/45.28; Qwen2.5-VL-72B 72.91/38.88/36.91; InternVL3-78B 72.16/32.19/34.72; Nanonets-OCR2-3B 68.42/42.27/42.77; MonkeyOCR-pro-1.2B 66.52/51.54/54.11; DeepSeek-OCR 64.27/73.84/69.94; PaddleOCR-VL 62.73/71.14/72.38; GPT-4o 59.32/48.53/50.03; GOT-OCR2 48.32/84.19/77.65; MinerU2.5-1.2B 21.33/125.59/124.65. Section 4.3 states Qwen3-VL-8B has the strongest aggregate score (paraphrase, data not prose).

claims.claim: Long multi-line handwritten maths, taken from over 6,000 authentic student answer sheets, degrades sharply for every model family and is far from reliably transcribed. Qwen3-VL-8B's F1 falls from 86.92 (ml-easy) to 70.45 (ml-hard) and its CER rises from 24.95 to 57.08. On ml-hard the best system by 1-NED (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) reaches only 55.81 (CER 54.91); GPT-4o scores 29.60 (CER 75.58), DeepSeek-OCR 42.24 (CER 70.71) and PaddleOCR-VL 41.78 (CER 83.51). Mean ground-truth length grows from 156.9 to 488.8 characters across easy to hard. Caveats: formulas are scored as LaTeX strings, which penalises equivalent markup, and GPT-4o's NED (weight 0.5) helped define the hard tier, which likely biases GPT-4o's ml-hard figure downward.
claims.quote: Table 7 (ml-hard; 1-NED / CER, %): Qwen2.5-VL-72B 55.81/54.91; Qwen3-VL-8B 50.54/57.08; InternVL3-78B 45.59/60.80; DeepSeek-OCR 42.24/70.71; PaddleOCR-VL 41.78/83.51; Nanonets-OCR2-3B 41.67/67.51; GPT-4o 29.60/75.58. Tables 6-7: Qwen3-VL-8B F1 86.92 (ml-easy) vs 70.45 (ml-hard), CER 24.95 vs 57.08. Table 2: mean label length 156.9 / 213.0 / 488.8 chars, LaTeX commands 4.1 / 7.6 / 25.7, lines 3.7 / 7.1 / 13.0 (easy / medium / hard). Data, not prose.

claims.claim: Generative models silently 'correct' what the student actually wrote, and several over-generate. The authors list four recurring errors: correcting writer mistakes, inserting plausible intermediate steps, dropping hard-to-read symbols, and drifting into Markdown or explanation. Figure 4 shows Qwen2.5-VL-72B and InternVL3-78B returning corrected but visually unsupported transcriptions of student maths. CER above 100% (insertions dominate) occurs for DeepSeek-VL2-27B on Chinese text (133.85), DeepSeek-OCR on single-line formulas (154.81), PaddleOCR-VL on single-line formulas (116.77) and MinerU2.5-1.2B overall (125.59). Implication for an auto-grader: a transcription step can turn a wrong answer into a right one before marking, so the pipeline needs faithfulness checks or human review.
claims.quote: Guo, Zhang & Jiang (2026), abstract: "several generative models hallucinate plausible but visually unsupported corrections". Supporting data: Table 5 DeepSeek-VL2-27B zh-text CER 133.85; Table 6 single-line CER DeepSeek-OCR 154.81 and PaddleOCR-VL 116.77; Table 4 MinerU2.5-1.2B CER 125.59.

claims.claim: Despite describing itself as testing multilingual handwriting, the benchmark holds only English text (GNHK 515 + IAM-line 11,344 = 11,859 images), Chinese text (CASIA-HWDB 11,655 + 874 private compositions = 12,529) and maths formulas. A full-text search of the PDF finds no Bengali, Bangla, Assamese, Hindi, Devanagari or Indic mention, and it reports no cost, price, latency or throughput figures, so it is no direct evidence on Indic-script accuracy or per-page cost. It does show rankings shift sharply by language: PaddleOCR-VL scores 1-NED 89.05 (CER 32.5) on Chinese but 73.66 (CER 47.48) on English; DeepSeek-OCR CER is 39.83 on English but 76.06 on Chinese; Gemma-3-27B-it 26.12 vs 95.18; Qwen2.5-VL-72B and Qwen3-VL-8B are best on Chinese (CER 10.42 and 11.89). A new script therefore needs its own validation.
claims.quote: Table 1 (composition: GNHK 515, IAM-line 11,344, CASIA-HWDB 11,655, private Chinese 874, CROHME 3,332, HME100K 9,754, MLHME 2,010 + 7,466, CC-OCR 100, private maths 30,522; total 77,572) and Table 5 (en-text / zh-text CER, %: PaddleOCR-VL 47.48/32.5; DeepSeek-OCR 39.83/76.06; Gemma-3-27B-it 26.12/95.18; GPT-4o 20.05/43.90; Qwen2.5-VL-72B 16.01/10.42; Qwen3-VL-8B 16.44/11.89). Data, not prose.

claims.claim: The headline numbers are not a neutral, independently replicated estimate. Public subsets were built by running Qwen2.5-VL-72B on about 160K samples and discarding those it found easy (about 46K kept). The hard/medium/easy tiers use a difficulty score weighting ground-truth length 0.2, complex LaTeX commands 0.3 and GPT-4o's NED 0.5. Every system got one short generic instruction with no per-model prompt tuning. Outputs were capped at 128 characters (single-line formulas) and 1024 characters (others). Formulas are scored as LaTeX strings, and the authors concede public subsets may be in pretraining data. The paper is arXiv v1 (19 Aug 2026) from East China Normal University, formatted for CIKM '26 (Rome, 7-11 Nov 2026) with a placeholder DOI, so acceptance is not confirmed. The benchmark release is promised in future tense, and the GitHub repo linked in the abstract returned HTTP 404 when checked on 8 Oct 2026 (org page returned 200), so the private student-sheet data cannot yet be verified. Use the figures as a ranking signal and re-test candidate engines on ExamLeaf's own Assamese, Bengali and Hindi sheets.
claims.quote: Method data (Sections 3.2.2 and 4.1): public pool 160K samples filtered to 46K using Qwen2.5-VL-72B NED; difficulty score weights 0.2 / 0.3 / 0.5 (length / complex LaTeX commands / GPT-4o NED); caps 128 and 1024 characters; 1-NED is the primary metric; release stated as 'will publicly release' (paraphrase). Link check on 2026-10-08: github.com/ECNU-RAIL/OmniHandwritingOCR-CIKM2026 returned 404. Data, not prose.

The price column has an input/output selector (per 1M tokens); the default view shows only the INPUT price, and the output price is in the page HTML. INR per 1M tokens, input/output: Qwen3 235B 63/247; Qwen3 32B 63/249; Qwen3 30B 24/77; Qwen2.5 VL 72B Instruct AWQ 106/108; DeepSeek V3 INT4 299/299; DeepSeek R1 INT4 484/484; MiniMax M1 41/188; OpenAI OSS 120B 23.50/23.50; Llama 4 Maverick 25/76; Gemma 3 27B 22/36. Output is about 3-4.6x input for the Qwen3, MiniMax and Llama 4 models, but equal to input for DeepSeek V3/R1 and Qwen2.5 VL. Dedicated VM per month: 1xH100 INR 196,113 on a 1-month term falling to INR 180,424 on a 1-year term (about 8% less, roughly INR 269 vs 247 per GPU-hour at 730 h); 1xL40S INR 80,221 falling to INR 73,803. For a 12-page paper that is INR 120 (Parsing) or INR 36 (Doc Ops) per sheet before any grading. My own estimate is INR 1.4-2.3 of token cost to grade a paper as text on Qwen3 235B at the rates above, assuming 10-25k input and 3k output tokens. The page lists no supported languages, no handwriting support and no accuracy figure, so it is pricing evidence only and does not show that Parsing or Doc Ops reads handwritten Assamese or Bengali.
claims.quote: Locator, not a verbatim quote: Partner AI Services section, Yotta Sarvam AI Services block (Sarvam Agent, Conversational AI, Analytics Services and Experts tabs), rows Parsing, Doc Ops, Mayura, Saarika, Bulbul.

claims.claim: Catalogue and capacity gaps found by absence checks on the raw page (retrieved 2026-10-07). Of the 21 token-priced Shakti Studio models, the only one labelled vision-language is Qwen2.5 VL 72B Instruct AWQ, an older generation than Qwen3-VL; Llama 4 Scout and Maverick appear without a vision label. The page names no dedicated OCR model (no DeepSeek-OCR, PaddleOCR, GOT-OCR, dots.ocr or MinerU), no GLM, Kimi, Hunyuan or InternVL, and no Indic-trained chat model such as Sarvam-M; Sarvam appears only as separate speech, translation and document services. The Studio platform entry (listed at INR 147,844 per GPU in the support-services table) says it supports custom or open-source models plus full fine-tuning and LoRA workflows, so newer OCR/VL models or an Indic fine-tune would have to be deployed on dedicated GPUs, not bought per token. The page gives no throughput, latency, rate-limit, concurrency or SLA figures for the token endpoints, so exam-season peak capacity would need a quote from the vendor.

The page footer calls Yotta India's sovereign cloud and AI infrastructure provider with hyperscale data centres in Navi Mumbai and Greater Noida, says its Yntraa Cloud is MeitY-empanelled, and describes Shakti Cloud as its NVIDIA-partnered AI service. The pricing page does not say which data centre serves a given Shakti Studio endpoint, whether prompts or images are logged or retained (the only retention figure is a 14-day default for backups), whether a data-processing agreement exists, or anything about the DPDP Act 2023 or children's data; the page source has zero mentions of DPDP, residency or GST. The MeitY empanelment is attributed to Yntraa Cloud, not explicitly to Shakti Studio. Treat it as a lead to verify contractually, not as compliance evidence.

claims.claim: CBSE's 2026 On-Screen Marking (OSM), mandated for Class 12 only by a 9 Feb 2026 circular (Class 10 stayed physical; Class 12 results out 13 May 2026), was human evaluators marking scanned scripts on a central portal at national scale: about 9.87 million answer sheets and about 70,000 evaluators. The article body never mentions AI, OCR, automated marking or privacy law (I checked the raw wikitext), so this is a case study of scanned-script pipeline, trust and security risks, not evidence on AI grading accuracy. Scale anchor for exam-season peak planning. Source is a Wikipedia compilation of press reports (page created 3 Jun 2026, last edited 10 Sep 2026).
claims.quote: 9,866,000 answer sheets were scanned and evaluated digitally by around 70,000 evaluators

claims.claim: Scan quality and script-to-student matching were the first visible failure modes: students who obtained their scanned copies reported blurred scans, missing pages and, in some cases, another student's sheet. Delhi student Vedant Shrivastava showed that his Physics sheet filed under his roll number carried different handwriting, and CBSE acknowledged the technical error and issued the correct sheet. Relevance for ExamLeaf: a phone-photo pipeline needs blur detection, page-count and page-sequence checks, and roll-number/identity binding before any OCR or grading, plus a path to flag a wrong or missing page.
claims.quote: blurred answer sheets, missing pages, and, in some cases, received another student's answer sheets

claims.claim: Security and data exposure undermined the system: CBSE first defended the portal as secure and robust, then admitted security gaps (the article's cited Moneycontrol headline of 31 May 2026 says it admitted gaps and that vulnerabilities were contained; a cited Hindu headline of 26 May says CBSE first refuted a compromise). 19-year-old ethical hacker Nisarga Adhikary, who reported to CERT-In, alleged that examiner accounts were reachable using public details and a password exposed in the code, and that answer sheets and question papers on an AWS server were publicly accessible through misconfiguration. The AWS and password points are allegations as reported, not an audit finding. Relevance: handling children's handwritten scripts in the DPDP era needs access-controlled storage, no secrets in code and an independent security audit; the article itself says nothing about privacy law.
claims.quote: it later admitted there were security gaps

claims.claim: Distrust turned into appeal volume and forced price cuts: after the pass percentage fell from 88.39% to 85.2% and students complained of unexpectedly low marks, especially in Physics, Chemistry, Biology and Mathematics, CBSE received 4,04,319 applications for scanned copies (the article reads this as lack of trust in the new system). It then cut fees from ₹700 to ₹100 per subject (scanned copy), from ₹500 to ₹100 per subject (verification) and from ₹100 to ₹25 per question (re-evaluation); students and teachers had criticised the fees. Relevance: a price and volume benchmark for an ExamLeaf human-review or appeal queue, and a warning that a grader students distrust floods the appeal channel.
claims.quote: fees for re-evaluation from ₹100 to ₹25 per question

claims.claim: Vendor and regulator precedent: the OSM contractor Coempt Eduteck is the renamed Globarena Technologies (CEO VSN Raju), which ran the 2019 Telangana Intermediate board evaluation after which over 380,000 of 970,000 students failed, with protests, reported student suicides and NHRC notices. Raju says a 2019 Supreme Court ruling calculated the actual evaluation error rate at 0.16% (the CEO's account as reported, not verified here), so a small measured error rate and a mass-failure scandal can coexist. In 2026 Ministry of Education reviews led to the removal of CBSE Chairman Rahul Singh and Secretary Himanshu Gupta (reported 2 Jun 2026 by The Hindu and Deccan Chronicle per the article's references), and Rahul Gandhi demanded a judicial probe. Relevance: vendor due diligence, and the political and human cost when high-stakes marking goes wrong.
claims.quote: over 380,000 out of 970,000 students failed their intermediate exams

result.publishDate: 2026-09-10 (last edited; page created 2026-06-03; cited press sources dated 2026-05-17 to 2026-06-03)

claims.claim: DPDP Rules 2025, Rule 15 neither bans nor whitelists foreign transfers of personal data. Transfer out of India is allowed, subject only to requirements the Central Government may later specify by general or special order for making data available to a foreign State, or to any entity under its control or any agency of it. The Rules contain no country list. The only localisation hook is Rule 13(4), which applies only to Significant Data Fiduciaries and only to data the Government later specifies.
claims.quote: may be transferred outside the territory of India subject to the restriction

claims.claim: Rule 10(1) requires verifiable parental consent before processing any child's personal data. The fiduciary must also do due diligence that the claimed parent is an identifiable adult (Rule 10(2)(a): someone who has completed eighteen years). It checks this against reliable identity and age details it already holds, or details or a virtual token from an authorised entity (DigiLocker-verified details count). Illustration cases 2 and 4 require that government-issued-detail or virtual-token check when the parent is not already a registered user.
claims.quote: verifiable consent of the parent is obtained before the processing

claims.claim: The child-data exemption is narrow. Rule 12 with Fourth Schedule Part A item 3 lifts Act sections 9(1) and 9(3) only for a Data Fiduciary that is an 'educational institution' (defined as an institution of learning that imparts education, including vocational education). It applies only to tracking and behavioural monitoring for its educational activities or children's safety. None of the six Part B purposes names exam marking or learning analytics, and no class is defined for third-party edtech or AI-grading vendors. Whether ExamLeaf could qualify as an educational institution is an open interpretation question.
claims.quote: for the educational activities of such institution

claims.claim: Rule 8(3) requires every Data Fiduciary (not just the large platforms in the Third Schedule) to retain personal data, associated traffic data and logs of processing for a minimum of one year from the date of processing before erasure, unless other law requires longer. This includes processing done on its behalf by a Data Processor. Its Illustration Case 2 says the fiduciary must ensure a cloud-provider processor also retains data and logs for at least one year. Rule 6(1)(e)-(f) separately requires one-year retention of logs and personal data for breach detection, and security-safeguard provisions in each Data Processor contract. Inference (not stated in the text): immediate-deletion or zero-retention designs conflict with these rules unless the fiduciary itself keeps the records.
claims.quote: for a minimum period of one year from the date of such processing

claims.claim: Rule 1(2)-(4) phases commencement. Rules 3 (notice), 5 to 16 (including security 6, breach intimation 7, retention 8, parental consent 10, child exemptions 12, Significant Data Fiduciary duties 13 and cross-border transfer 15), 22 and 23 take effect eighteen months after the Gazette's publication (notification dated 13 November 2025, so about mid-May 2027). Rule 4 (Consent Managers) takes effect one year after (about November 2026). Rules 1, 2 and 17 to 21 (Board machinery) take effect on publication.
claims.quote: Rules 3, 5 to 16, 22 and 23 shall come into force eighteen months

claims.claim: WildHandBench (Zhang et al., arXiv 2608.22959 v1, 24 Aug 2026; 500 wild handwritten documents, Chinese/English) finds dedicated OCR models behind general-purpose VLMs. The best of the 11 OCR specialists, PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 (0.9B), scores 54.21 Overall (GLM-OCR 54.06, MinerU2.5-Pro 51.73, HunyuanOCR 51.44, dots.mocr 49.97, dots.ocr 43.73) against 71.85 for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and the top six models are all general-purpose. DeepSeek-OCR2 (3B-A0.5B) collapses to 9.46 Overall (free-text edit distance 91.70, table TEDS 1.77) and the paper offers no explanation. The gap is not uniform: on free text alone HunyuanOCR (edit distance 38.50) and PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 (41.52) beat Claude Opus 4.8 (53.30) and InternVL3.5 (46.80).
claims.quote: "fall behind general VLMs on wild handwriting" (Zhang et al., WildHandBench, Main Results). Table 2 Overall column: Gemini 3.1 Pro 71.85, PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 54.21, GLM-OCR 54.06, DeepSeek-OCR2 9.46.

claims.claim: Chinese open-weight general VLMs (listed as open general models) sit close to the proprietary leaders: Kimi-K3 (2.8T total, 104B active) 67.81 Overall, Qwen3.5-Plus (397B-A17B) 65.55, Qwen3-VL (235B-A22B) 62.19, versus Gemini 3.1 Pro 71.85, Gemini 3.5 Flash 68.25 and Claude Opus 4.8 57.70. Kimi-K3's free-text edit distance (26.07) beats Gemini 3.5 Flash (27.10) and trails Gemini 3.1 Pro (24.32) by 1.75. Not every Chinese VLM does well: InternVL3.5 (241B-A28B) scores only 52.80. Gemini 3.5 Flash is just 3.60 points behind Gemini 3.1 Pro. The winners are very large MoE models, and the paper reports no price, token, latency or throughput figures, so accuracy per dollar cannot be derived from it.
claims.quote: Table 2 data (Overall / free-text edit distance, lower is better): Gemini 3.1 Pro 71.85 / 24.32; Gemini 3.5 Flash 68.25 / 27.10; Kimi-K3 67.81 / 26.07; Qwen3.5-Plus 65.55 / 34.80; Qwen3-VL 62.19 / 34.30; Claude Opus 4.8 57.70 / 53.30; InternVL3.5 52.80 / 46.80.

claims.claim: Model errors are mostly prior-driven: the model outputs a fluent, more probable string instead of what is written (its output has lower perplexity than the ground truth under a reference LM), while humans tend to give partial, cautious transcriptions of illegible content. Overall PDE runs from 63.28% (GLM-OCR) and 64.48% (PaddleOCR-VL-1.6) up to 90.80% (DeepSeek-OCR2), with Gemini 3.1 Pro at 77.51%, versus 49.27% for humans. The abstract states 63-91% but the Conclusion states 63-79%, which matches excluding DeepSeek-OCR2, so the paper states the range inconsistently. On formulas 87.83-98.35% of model errors are prior-driven (Gemini 3.1 Pro 94.77%) versus 46.36% for humans. Implication for ExamLeaf (my inference, not tested in the paper): a transcription stage could silently fix a student's wrong word or maths step toward the expected answer and inflate marks. The authors caution that PDE describes error type, not error rate, and depends on Qwen3-8B-Base as the reference model.
claims.quote: Table 2 PDE columns (data): Overall PDE 63.28 GLM-OCR; 64.48 PaddleOCR-VL-1.6; 71.94 Kimi-K3; 77.51 Gemini 3.1 Pro; 79.21 Gemini 3.5 Flash; 90.80 DeepSeek-OCR2; Human 49.27. Formula PDE: models 87.83 to 98.35, Human 46.36.

claims.claim: Even the best model stays below the human baseline overall (71.85 vs 77.09), but unevenly. On tables the best TEDS is 60.44 versus human 74.78 (over 14 points); on formulas the best CDM is 79.42 (Gemini 3.1 Pro) versus human 86.56; on free text three models (Gemini 3.1 Pro 24.32, Kimi-K3 26.07, Gemini 3.5 Flash 27.10) beat the human edit distance of 30.08. Open OCR specialists reach at most 63.11 CDM on formulas (FireRed-OCR). The formula and table subsets are small (52 and 81 images) so differences between close models are weak, and the annotators were native Chinese speakers, which the authors say may understate human accuracy on cursive English handwriting.
claims.quote: Table 2 data, Human row: free-text edit 30.08, table TEDS 74.78, formula CDM 86.56, Overall 77.09; best model per column: 24.32, 60.44, 79.42, 71.85 (all Gemini 3.1 Pro).

claims.claim: The paper gives no direct evidence for ExamLeaf's languages or documents. Its four language settings are Simplified Chinese 66.6%, English 28.6%, Traditional Chinese 2.6% and Chinese-English mixed 2.2% of 500 samples, so there is no Assamese, Bengali or Devanagari, and no school answer sheets (scenarios include calligraphy, poetry, historical archives and medical notes, plus an Education and learning group of 61 documents). It reports no per-language, per-scenario or per-degradation scores, no cost, latency or token numbers, and gives no dataset or code link. GOT-OCR, Qwen2.5-VL and GLM-4.xV are not among the 18 models. It is an arXiv v1 preprint (CC BY 4.0, no venue listed). I cross-checked every Table 2 row against the paper's Overall formula and all match within rounding, but absolute scores should not be transferred to Indic exam scripts.
claims.quote: Benchmark Taxonomy, language counts (data): Simplified Chinese 333, English 143, Traditional Chinese 13, Chinese-English mixed 11, total 500. Limitations (data): 500 samples, formula subset 52 images, table subset 81 images, focus primarily on Chinese and English. Table 4 scenario counts sum to 500.

claims.claim: In UC Irvine's 2025 calculus-quiz deployment (English handwriting, maths transcribed to LaTeX), a general multimodal LLM used as the OCR step (GPT-4.1-mini, prompted with the problem statement) beat the specialist maths-OCR product Mathpix on a hard 171-solution subset: 84% of transcriptions rated acceptable versus 55%, and about 88% acceptable over thousands of submissions (Yu et al., Sec. 3). 'Acceptable' includes transcriptions merely sufficient for rubric grading; the paper reports no character or word error rates and does not name or score the other OCR options the authors say they tried first.
claims.quote: "GPT-4.1-mini achieved 84% acceptable transcriptions, compared to 55% for Mathpix." (Yu et al., arXiv:2603.00895, Sec. 3)

claims.claim: Against official teaching-assistant scores on 3,945 handwritten free-response records (Spring 2025, Math 2A and 2B), AI scores averaged 0.40 points lower (SD 1.12). Per-quiz mean absolute error ranged 0.5 to 1.06 points (questions in the paper's worked examples carry about 3 to 5 points), and 68% to 86% of AI scores per quiz were within 1 point of the TA score. AI scores were advisory only; TA grades stayed official. The human benchmark is also loose: two independent human reviewers using the same rubric gave identical scores on only about 45% of the 171-solution hard subset.
claims.quote: [Locator, not a verbatim quote: Sec. 6.1.1-6.1.2 and Figs. 3-4; Appendix A.10.4 and Fig. 10]

claims.claim: An independent audit of 3,851 AI-graded records (Math 2A: 1,819; Math 2B: 2,032) by 20+ reviewers (graduate students, undergraduates and advanced high-school students) rated 79.79% of AI evaluations fully correct, 9.55% acceptable and 10.67% incorrect. Input/OCR quality was rated acceptable for 87.64% and problematic for 12.36%, and over 90% of AI-minus-reviewer score gaps were within 1 point. The two named error patterns were over-penalising valid methods absent from the rubric, and undue leniency toward answers that follow familiar rubric steps but contain incorrect reasoning.
claims.quote: [Locator, not a verbatim quote: Sec. 6.3 and Figs. 5-7]

claims.claim: Reported failure modes and mitigations for LLM-based handwriting transcription: with blank or sparse answer boxes GPT-4.1-mini invents full solutions, suppressed by pre-printing 'Solution' and 'Final Answer' labels in each box and stating the question in the OCR prompt; it still auto-corrected students' mistakes in under 2% of samples despite an explicit instruction not to; the final-answer box is more error-prone than the working area because it offers little context; crossed-out work is hard (prompts that suppressed it also dropped valid nearby ink); diagrams are poorly handled (GPT-4.1-mini limited, Mathpix reconstructed none); of the 27 problematic transcriptions in the 171-solution subset the dominant cause was nested or complex fractions. OCR and grading run per question region, not per whole page, to limit cross-problem interference and hallucination.
claims.quote: [Locator, not a verbatim quote: Sec. 2, Sec. 3, Sec. 4.2 and Appendix A.2 to A.5]

claims.claim: The authors have no validated human-review policy: they state they lack a systematic rule for when to trust the AI versus defer to a human, and use only hand-built triggers (a correct final answer receiving less than full credit; high run-to-run variance, e.g. o3-mini run three times and flagged for review when exactly one run gives full credit). Only low-stakes quizzes (about 10% of course grade) were covered, and the authors say midterms and finals would need substantially more conservative human-in-the-loop controls; surveyed students (n=301) called for human oversight and only 60-61% rated the feedback very or mostly accurate. Scope limits for ExamLeaf: only OpenAI models and Mathpix tested, English-language single-variable calculus at one US university, no Indic scripts, no Chinese or open-weight models, no cost or latency figures, and no comparison with grading directly from the page image.
claims.quote: [Locator, not a verbatim quote: Sec. 5 'Human review', Sec. 6.2, Sec. 7 'Intervention policy', 'High-stakes deployment' and 'Scope']

claims.claim: As of the 7 Oct 2026 snapshot, several Chinese vision-capable models match or beat pricier Western ones on the Artificial Analysis intelligence_index embedded in each entry (a general-intelligence score, not a grading, handwriting or Indic-script test): z-ai/glm-5.3-flash scores 41.8 at $0.15 input / $0.50 output per million tokens (text+image+video input, 1,048,576-token context), xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-pro 46.3 at $0.435/$0.87, moonshotai/kimi-k3 43.6 at $0.50/$15.00 and deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash 39.5 at $0.30/$1.20, against google/gemini-3.8-flash 40.9 at $0.75/$3.75, openai/gpt-6-luna 38.1 at $0.10/$0.50 and anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 56 at $2/$10. GLM-5.3-Flash therefore scores slightly above Gemini 3.8 Flash at 5x lower input and 7.5x lower output price, but its reasoning is mandatory with default effort 'max', so billed output will include thinking tokens; qwen/qwen3.7-flash, qwen/qwen3.8-flash and anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 have no score listed.

claims.claim: Per the Handbook's reading of the DPDP Act and the November 2025 Rules, sending personal data outside India is permitted by default. The Government may bar transfers to particular countries by notification (s.16(1)). The Rules can attach conditions, notably where foreign governments or government-controlled entities are involved (Rule 15). For Significant Data Fiduciaries, a Government committee can recommend categories of personal data that may not leave India (Rule 13(4)). The Handbook names no restricted country and treats sector-specific localisation (its example is RBI payment data) as a separate regime. As summarised in January 2026, an ordinary fiduciary therefore has no blanket localisation duty unless a country notification or sector rule applies.
claims.quote: Paraphrase, not verbatim. Handbook p.16, Summary of Law item 6 (transfers outside India), with footnotes 45-48 (DPDP Act s.16(1); Rules 13(4) and 15; RBI payment-data storage direction). Significant Data Fiduciary designation is described on p.15.

claims.claim: The Handbook states that a fiduciary must obtain verifiable parental consent before processing a child's personal data (s.9(1)). It may not track, behaviourally monitor or target advertising at children, even with parental consent, unless a Rules exception applies. The exceptions it lists include educational institutions monitoring students' data for academic purposes and safety, plus health-care, email-account management, harmful-content prevention and age-verification uses. It does not say whether a private ed-tech platform counts as an educational institution, so per-student analytics or tracking by such a platform is an open compliance question. The Rules do not prescribe a consent method: a business may use reliable parent identity and age details it already holds, or details or tokens issued by government-authorised entities. The Handbook says the Act's substantive provisions take effect in May 2027, an 18-month runway after the Rules were published in November 2025.
claims.quote: Paraphrase, not verbatim. Handbook p.15 (children and persons with disabilities), pp.34-35 (Using children's data; parental-consent methods; bar on tracking and behavioural monitoring; listed exceptions; footnotes 118-121), and p.12 (Rules of November 2025; substantive provisions from May 2027).

claims.claim: The Handbook says the DPDP Act has no equivalent of GDPR Article 22. Individuals have no formal right to challenge fully automated decisions, and organisations are not legally required to involve humans or offer recourse. It calls human oversight good practice and a hedge against future AI regulation. Separately, its education example says developers of AI exam-grading tools need systems that can explain the rationale for a score and let students contest results, with continuous monitoring so no group of students is unfairly advantaged or disadvantaged. It also recommends grievance portals with multi-tier escalation to human reviewers. These are best-practice recommendations (the education point is cited to a 2024 paper on AI rubric assessment in higher education), not statutory duties.
claims.quote: "The DPDP Act does not include an equivalent to GDPR’s Article 22" (Handbook p.45, Individuals' rights, Differences with other laws). The education-sector grading guidance is paraphrased from p.71 (footnotes 305-306); the human-escalation and grievance-portal advice is paraphrased from p.73.

claims.claim: The Handbook places legal responsibility on the fiduciary (here, ExamLeaf), including for its processors' actions. The Act sets no specific obligations or penalties for processors, so duties such as purpose limitation, security, sub-processors, breach handling and indemnity must be imposed by contract. Penalties of up to INR 250 crore (about USD 30 million) can be levied on a fiduciary for failing to secure personal data, processing without proper consent, or not meeting the extra children's-data obligations, with no criminal liability. Its LLM-API example treats an app owner and an AI model provider reached through an API as potentially joint fiduciaries where they jointly decide how user data is used (for example log retention and fine-tuning). This illustrates that a provider which retains or trains on submitted data may not be a mere processor.
claims.quote: Paraphrase, not verbatim. Handbook p.16 (processors: no specific obligations or penalties; duties passed on by contract), p.17 (penalties up to INR 250 crore, USD 30 million; no criminal liability), pp.39-41 (fiduciary versus processor roles; Example 4 on an app owner and a model provider accessed via API as possible joint fiduciaries; contract checklist).

claims.claim: On consent mechanics, the Handbook says consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous. Notices must be offered in English and in languages recognised in the Constitution (s.5(3)). Withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent and may require halting further training use. Data collected for one purpose may not be reusable for AI training on the original consent, so fresh notice and consent may be needed. Its ed-tech proctoring example flags that making consent to model training a condition of taking an exam may fail the freely-given test. Implication, not stated in the Handbook: reusing students' handwritten scripts to fine-tune OCR or grading models would need separate, unbundled consent, parental for minors.
claims.quote: Paraphrase, not verbatim. Handbook p.14 (notice in English and Constitution-recognised languages; footnote 20), p.33 (form of consent; ed-tech proctoring example; purpose specification and re-use for AI training), p.34 (withdrawal of consent as easy as giving it; footnotes 114-116).

claims.claim: IIIT-Indic-HW-UC is a phone-camera (not flatbed-scanned) handwriting dataset: 91K page images in 13 Indic languages including Assamese, Bengali and Hindi, from 1,220 writers, with 2,600K word images (566,187 unique words), 7K pages and 200K word images per language, and page-level annotation (word boxes, reading order, transcription, language of each word).
claims.quote: [data readout, abstract and 'IIIT-Indic-HW-UC Dataset' section] 91K page images; 13 languages incl. Assamese, Bengali, Hindi; 1,220 writers; 2600K words; 566,187 unique words; 7K pages and 200K word images per language; mobile camera instead of flatbed scanner.

claims.claim: On the dataset's own camera-captured test split, recognisers trained on it score (CRR/WRR, higher is better): Assamese 90.98/85.15, Bengali 96.60/89.10 (96.69/89.27 when also trained on the older IIIT-INDIC-HW-WORDS set), Hindi 93.88/84.69 (93.96/85.06). Even a purpose-trained recogniser therefore misreads roughly 11-15% of words, and these are word-level results (the page says the benchmark focuses on word recognition), not end-to-end page results. Assamese has no result on the older set (the dash in the table), so this is the only Assamese entry in the comparison.
claims.quote: [data readout, Table 3 image at img/projects/recognition/ucciohd/t003.jpg, IIIT-Indic-HW-UC test columns] Assamese 90.98 CRR / 85.15 WRR; Bengali 96.60/89.10 (UC-only), 96.69/89.27 (Both); Hindi 93.88/84.69 (UC-only), 93.96/85.06 (Both). The table is an image, not page text.

claims.claim: Recognisers trained only on the older IIIT-INDIC-HW-WORDS set lose heavily on this camera-captured test set: Bengali WRR 84.29 -> 51.51 (CRR 95.72 -> 79.66) and Hindi WRR 83.09 -> 40.81 (CRR 96.08 -> 72.27). Training on the camera data restores camera-test WRR (Bengali 89.10, Hindi 84.69) but lowers accuracy on the old set (Bengali 53.82, Hindi 63.65). Cross-dataset generalisation is poor (the table cannot separate camera effects from writer and content differences), so fine-tuning on phone-photo handwriting matters for ExamLeaf.
claims.quote: [data readout, Table 3 image, rows by training set] trained on IIIT-INDIC-HW-WORDS: Bengali tested on old set 95.72/84.29, on UC 79.66/51.51; Hindi 96.08/83.09 vs 72.27/40.81. Trained on UC: tested on old set Bengali 85.99/53.82, Hindi 89.66/63.65.

claims.claim: The benchmark content differs from school answer sheets: each page holds one corpus-derived paragraph of at most 50 words on an A4 white page, the listed content types are alphabetic and numeric, and a significant share of the contributors are aged 20-40 (70% female, 854 of 1,220). The page describes no mathematical or chemical notation, diagrams, ruled answer-book paper or school-age (15-18) writers and reports no under-18 share, so these scores are probably optimistic for ExamLeaf (the last point is my inference).
claims.quote: "featuring diverse content types, such as alphabetic and numeric" (abstract, Mondal and Jawahar, IIIT-Indic-HW-UC page). Other details are data readouts from the 'Data Collection and Annotation' and 'Writer Characteristics' sections: at most 50 words per paragraph, one per A4 white page, age band 20-40, 854 female and 366 male writers.

claims.claim: Per-language zips are directly downloadable from cvit.iiit.ac.in (Assamese about 4.26 GB, Bengali 7.92 GB, Hindi 3.58 GB, Marathi 3.01 GB; server Last-Modified 30 Jul 2024), with a 150K/20K/30K train/validation/test word-image split per language. However the page states no licence or terms of use, its 'Code' entry is plain unlinked text, and the page is an outdated pre-publication copy (venue field blank, BibTeX 'Updated Soon', abstract promises release after acceptance; ICPR 2024 per ilocr.iiit.ac.in/publication). Rights for commercial fine-tuning would need written confirmation from IIIT Hyderabad.

A page scan found no licence wording. Split figures from the 'Dataset Splits' section: 75% (150K), 10% (20K), 15% (30K) per language.

result.publishDate: 2024 (the page itself is undated and its venue field is blank; ICPR 2024 per ilocr.iiit.ac.in/publication; dataset zips last-modified 2024-07-30)

claims.claim: Scope gap: the paper trains and tests only Hindi, Bengali, Tamil and Telugu handwritten pages. The string Assam never appears in the 17-page text, nor do maths, equations, chemical formulae, diagrams or exam answer scripts, and mixed-script documents are listed as future work. None of its error rates therefore measure Assamese, English+maths, or student-exam handwriting. Bengali is the nearest proxy (outside knowledge, not stated by the authors: Assamese is written in the Bengali-Assamese script, in the same Unicode block).
claims.quote: Sec. 6 Conclusion (p.16) of Bhattacharyya, Mondal, Jawahar: "Future work will focus on severe degradations, mixed-script documents, and layout-aware modeling". Also, the Abstract (p.1) and Sec. 6 name exactly four languages: Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu.

claims.claim: Zero-shot Chinese open-weight models are unusable on full handwritten Indic pages. On 500 test pages per language, DeepSeek-OCR scores WER/CER 4.19/3.80 (Hindi), 7.00/8.02 (Bengali), 1.41/1.91 (Tamil), 25.68/17.14 (Telugu). Qwen2-VL-2B has WER 1.79-5.62 and Qwen2.5-VL-3B WER 1.15-6.75; a WER above 1.0 means more edits than reference words, i.e. runaway or hallucinated output. PaddleOCR has WER 0.93-0.96 and CER 0.67-0.84 on Hindi, Tamil and Telugu, with no Bengali result. Caveats: only the 2B/3B Qwen sizes were tested (not Qwen3-VL, GLM-4.xV, InternVL, PaddleOCR-VL, dots.ocr or MinerU), and baseline checkpoints and prompts are unspecified, so larger or newer models cannot be inferred from this. The best free non-Chinese baseline, Chandra OCR, reaches WER 0.23 (Hindi), 0.36 (Bengali), 0.56 (Tamil), 0.89 (Telugu).
claims.quote: Not verbatim; numbers from Table 1 (p.8) and Table 2 (p.9), WER then CER. DeepSeek-OCR: Hindi 4.1910 3.7953; Bengali 6.9971 8.0158; Tamil 1.4124 1.9058; Telugu 25.6800 17.1386. Qwen2-VL-2B WER: 2.3004, 1.7860, 4.6471, 5.6157. Qwen2.5-VL-3B WER: 4.9442, 2.7089, 6.7536, 1.1500. PaddleOCR: Hindi 0.9612 0.8413; Tamil 0.9542 0.6723; Telugu 0.9324 0.7533; Bengali dash. Sec. 4.1 (p.8-9) attributes the failures to zero-shot or prompt-based use on long handwriting.

claims.claim: Commercial engines lead on handwritten Indic pages, and a LoRA-adapted open model comes within a few WER points. WER/CER: Sarvam OCR 0.0682/0.0419 (Hindi), 0.0542/0.0194 (Bengali), 0.0382/0.0189 (Tamil), 0.0331/0.0221 (Telugu). Gemini Flash (version unstated) 0.0708/0.0447, 0.0584/0.0211, 0.0428/0.0207, 0.0377/0.0246, i.e. about 0.3-0.5 WER points behind Sarvam. IndicPage-OCR 0.0823/0.0466, 0.0719/0.0221, 0.0855/0.0266, 0.0426/0.0292, i.e. about 1.0-4.7 WER points behind Sarvam. Even the best system mis-reads roughly 3-7% of words, on prose pages from the authors' in-house digitization data, not exam answers. Caveats: the abstract headline (gap cut about 80% in WER, over 90% in CER) matches the arithmetic of the single illustrative page in Fig. 1 (free-OCR average WER 0.5000, commercial 0.0863, IndicPage-OCR 0.1667), not the 500-page tables; Fig. 1's caption says Bengali but the page shown is Devanagari; Table 3 and the text differ from Tables 1-2 by up to 0.0011.

Adding a script with this recipe is cheap in compute but not in data. The method freezes GOT-OCR 2.0's vision encoder and connector, applies LoRA (rank 8, alpha 32) to its Qwen-0.5B decoder only, and trains one adapter per language on 1024x1024 input. It used a single RTX 6000 Ada GPU (batch 4, about 200K steps to converge). REFUTATION FAILED. I read the full primary PDF (17 pp, extracted with pdftotext and visually checked pp.7 and 12). Every checkable element of the claim matches. Crossref shows the same title as a peer-reviewed Springer LNCS chapter (DAS 2026, pp.317-333, published online 2026-08-28). The project page also says "Accepted at DAS 2026". So the source is primary, peer-reviewed and current.

VERIFIED
- Sec 3.1 (p.5): input resized to 1024x1024; initialised from the GOT-OCR 2.0 checkpoint; Qwen-0.5B decoder.
- Sec 3.2 (p.6): vision encoder frozen, linear connector unchanged. LoRA on the decoder's linear layers excluding the LM head, r=8, alpha=32. A separate model per language.
- Sec 3.4 (p.7): in-house dataset. Pages: Hindi 23,912; Bengali 7,189; Telugu 6,121; Tamil 5,454. Existing word-level annotations are used to build word crops and to derive line samples by grouping words per line. About 12 million samples after augmentation; about 1.5 million train+val; fixed 500-page test set per language.
- Sec 3.5 (p.7): single RTX 6000 Ada, batch 4, converged by about 200K steps.
- Table 3 (p.12), WER/CER, page-only vs progressive:
  - Hindi 0.521/0.312 vs 0.0813/0.0455
  - Bengali 0.488/0.284 vs 0.0721/0.0226
  - Tamil 0.612/0.352 vs 0.0844/0.0261
  - Telugu 0.437/0.261 vs 0.0416/0.0283
  So the stated ranges 0.437-0.612 and 0.0416-0.0844 are exact.
- "Not reported" holds. There are no GPU-hours or dollars. No full fine-tuning experiment. No zero-shot GOT-OCR 2.0 row: Tables 1-2 compare only Sarvam, Gemini Flash, Chandra, DeepSeek-OCR, Qwen2-VL-2B, Qwen2.5-VL-3B, olmOCR, PaddleOCR, Tesseract and EasyOCR.
- The abstract points to indicpageocr.github.io. That page shows "Code Coming Soon" and no dataset release. Hugging Face has four per-language models (indicpage-ocr-hindi, -bengali, -tamil, -telugu), which corroborates one adapter per language.

QUALIFICATIONS (real, but they do not flip the verdict)
1. Table 3 compares page-only against word->line->page. The page-only arm never sees the roughly 1.5M word/line samples, so the gap confounds ordering with extra word/line supervision. The same group's ICDAR 2025 HindiOCR-VLM paper (Table 5) ran a controlled test on identical data. Mixed training reached WRR 82.40 at 800k steps; progressive reached 84.74 at 350k steps. Ordering therefore gives a modest gain and faster convergence, while the 5-10x WER gap in Table 3 mostly reflects word/line data. Read "curriculum essential" as "word/line supervision essential"; that still supports the claim's last sentence. Line labels are derived from position-aware word annotations, not separately annotated. The paper does not say how the 200K steps split across phases, and 200K steps at batch 4 is about 33-147 epochs over the page-only pages.
2. Sec 3.4 gives the 12M and 1.5M figures as "overall" for all four languages combined, not per language. The claim's wording "Data per language ... plus ... 12 million" invites a per-language misreading.
3. "Cheap in compute" is an inference, which the claim itself flags by listing GPU-hours as unreported. Inference is slow: 12.42 s/page, 0.08 pages/s, 5 GB, on an RTX 6000 Ada. The Hindi predecessor used 2xA6000, batch 16, 350k steps.
4. Tables 1-2 give slightly different IndicPage numbers from Table 3 and the text (Hindi WER 0.0823 vs 0.0813; Tamil 0.0855 vs 0.0844), unexplained. Several baseline WERs exceed 1 (DeepSeek-OCR Telugu 25.68), which suggests untuned baselines. The test sets are in-house and unreleased, with no independent replication and no Assamese.
5. Context: a community GOT-OCR2 LoRA Telugu model trained on about 80K word crops reports CER 0.31 and WER 0.85. That is a different task and data, and consistent with "not cheap in data".

Verdict: specifics are accurate, the source is primary, peer-reviewed and current, and the claim itself discloses the gaps. Not refuted. Downstream text should say "word/line supervision" rather than "ordering", and should not read 12M/1.5M as per-language.

1. Rankings are task-dependent (abstract and Sec 4.4).
 - By 1-NED, Qwen3-VL-8B is first only on Chinese text and ml-medium.
 - On English text it is a three-way tie: Nanonets 84.96, Qwen3-VL-8B 84.76, Qwen2.5-VL-72B 84.63. This is the subset closest to ExamLeaf.
 - On single-line formulas it is 74.20, behind MonkeyOCR-pro 87.56 and Kimi-VL 93.60.
 - So "well ahead of every dedicated OCR model" holds only in the aggregate.
2. The ">2x CER" for DeepSeek-OCR and PaddleOCR-VL is driven by over-generation.
 - CER on single-line formulas is 154.81 and 116.77. The paper says insertions dominate.
 - On Chinese text PaddleOCR-VL beats Qwen3-VL-8B on BLEU-4 (81.39 vs 72.24) and F1 (91.65 vs 88.72).
 - DeepSeek-OCR's CER is only 1.24-1.53x Qwen3-VL-8B's on the three multi-line formula subsets.
 - PaddleOCR-VL is designed for task prompts such as "OCR:" and "Formula Recognition:" (arXiv 2510.14528), so one generic instruction may handicap it.
 - That report gives its own handwriting edit distances of 0.089 (Chinese) and 0.042 (English). These are vendor figures on a different dataset.
3. The benchmark is built with models in the loop.
 - Public samples were filtered to those Qwen2.5-VL-72B got wrong.
 - Difficulty tiers use GPT-4o NED at weight 0.5, which exaggerates the GPT-4o gap (1-NED falls from 71.17 on ml-easy to 29.60 on ml-hard).
 - The pre-annotation model is unnamed.
 - The authors concede public subsets may be in pretraining data.
4. The result is a snapshot. The only closed model is GPT-4o (2024), with no Gemini, GPT-5 or Claude. Successors DeepSeek-OCR 2 (arXiv 2601.20552) and PaddleOCR-VL-1.5 (arXiv 2601.21957), both Jan 2026, were not tested. Table 4 also differs slightly from the mean of the subset tables for the two models in question: DeepSeek-OCR WER 69.94 vs 65.27, PaddleOCR-VL CER 71.14 vs 74.79. Neither gap changes the >2x conclusion.
5. It is not independently reproducible yet. The promised repo github.com/ECNU-RAIL/OmniHandwritingOCR-CIKM2026 returns 404 as of 8 Oct 2026 and is not among the organisation's 37 public repos. The paper only says data "will" be released. My web-search budget was exhausted, so I searched via the arXiv API and direct fetches and found no replication and no direct rebuttal.
6. Independent evidence on a different task also limits how far "best" generalises. EDU-CIRCUIT-HW (ACL 2026 Findings, arXiv 2602.00095, real STEM student handwriting, six models) ranks Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking last on sample error rate at 85.43%. The others are Gemini-3-Preview 37.62%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 53.52%, Qwen3-VL-Plus 61.72%, GPT-5.1 71.54% and Claude-4.5-Sonnet 80.70%. "Best" therefore applies only to the 13 systems tested.

Suggested safe wording: "In the unweighted six-subtask mean, Qwen3-VL-8B led all 13 systems; on English handwriting alone it was tied with Nanonets-OCR2-3B and Qwen2.5-VL-72B."

I could not refute the claim. It reports the primary source (arXiv 2608.22959) accurately, and the paper is current and still v1. The only wording issues are minor. I could not run a third-party search for disputes because the WebSearch budget was exhausted at 200/200.

SOURCE CHECK
- arxiv.org/abs/2608.22959 exists. Title: "WildHandBench: A Benchmark for Handwritten Text Understanding that Challenges MLLMs and Humans". First author: Jun Zhang.
- Submission history lists only v1, Mon 24 Aug 2026 08:25:12 UTC. The /abs/...v2 URL returns 404. The arXiv API shows published and updated dates both as 24 Aug 2026. Licence is CC BY 4.0. There is no journal reference.
- That is 45 days before today (8 Oct 2026), so the claim is not outdated.
- Every figure below comes from the paper's Table 2, extracted twice from arxiv.org/html/2608.22959[v1] with different prompts. The two extractions agreed.

NUMBERS
- Table 2 covers 18 models: 3 proprietary, 4 open general VLMs and 11 open OCR models.
- Every figure in the claim matches Table 2:
  - Gemini 3.1 Pro: Overall 71.85.
  - PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 (0.9B): Overall 54.21, free-text edit distance 41.52.
  - GLM-OCR: 54.06.
  - MinerU2.5-Pro: 51.73.
  - HunyuanOCR: 51.44, edit distance 38.50.
  - dots.mocr: 49.97.
  - dots.ocr: 43.73.
  - DeepSeek-OCR2 (3B-A0.5B): Overall 9.46, edit distance 91.70, TEDS 1.77.
  - Claude Opus 4.8 edit distance: 53.30.
  - InternVL3.5 edit distance: 46.80.
- I recomputed Overall as ((100-edit)+TEDS+CDM)/3 for all 19 rows, including the human baseline. All match to within 0.02, so the extracted table is internally consistent.
- Ranking by Overall: Gemini 3.1 Pro 71.85, Gemini 3.5 Flash 68.25, Kimi-K3 67.81, Qwen3.5-Plus 65.55, Qwen3-VL 62.19, Claude Opus 4.8 57.70. All six are general-purpose, and PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 is 7th.
- The paper's Main Results text says the same: "OCR-focused models ... fall behind general VLMs on wild handwriting. The top six models on WildHandBench are all general-purpose".
- Languages: Simplified Chinese 333 (66.6%), English 143 (28.6%), Traditional Chinese 13, Chinese-English mixed 11. "Chinese/English" is a fair shorthand.

"NO EXPLANATION" SUB-CLAIM
- The paper never names DeepSeek-OCR2 in its analysis.
- The strings repetition, loop, truncat, fail, collapse and hallucinat do not appear anywhere in the text.
- The only related text is generic and unnamed. The Error Pattern Analysis section says "Among models with functional visual encoders, PDE rates range from 63% to 79%". It then says "At the extreme, models with severely limited visual decoding produce almost exclusively prior-driven errors". The abstract's "63-91%" prior-driven-error range implicitly treats DeepSeek-OCR2 (PDE 90.80) as the extreme.
- That describes the symptom and gives no root cause, so "offers no explanation" holds, though it is slightly strong.

MINOR IMPRECISIONS (verdict unchanged)
- The parenthetical list skips FireRed-OCR (52.82) and Qianfan-OCR (52.07). Both rank above MinerU2.5-Pro, HunyuanOCR and dots.*, so the list is not a ranking.
- "OCR models behind general VLMs" holds for 6 of 7 general models. General-purpose InternVL3.5 (52.80) is itself below PaddleOCR-VL-1.6, GLM-OCR and FireRed-OCR. The best OCR model trails Claude Opus 4.8 by only 3.5 points.
- Five general models still beat HunyuanOCR's 38.50 on free text: Gemini 3.1 Pro 24.32, Kimi-K3 26.07, Gemini 3.5 Flash 27.10, Qwen3-VL 34.30 and Qwen3.5-Plus 34.80. The "not uniform" exception is therefore limited to the two weakest general models.
- The supplied "supporting quote" covers only the headline and four numbers. The rest is confirmed in Table 2, not in the quote.

CAVEATS ON WEIGHT (not grounds to refute)
- It is a single unreviewed v1 preprint with no affiliations listed in the document.
- It has only 500 samples. The authors say it "should not be interpreted as a population-level estimate", and "focuses primarily on Chinese and English handwriting".
- It contains no Hindi, Bengali, Assamese or Devanagari, so it must not be used as evidence for Indic OCR.
- The harness used temperature 0.0 and max 8192 output tokens, with DeepSeek-OCR-v2 run through local vLLM on its "recommended prompt settings". The 9.46 may be a harness artifact rather than true model capability. That is my inference and is unverified.
- No corrections or conflicting numbers turned up in the direct checks. The v2 URL and the Hugging Face papers page both return 404, and the PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 model card and DeepSeek-OCR-2 README make no handwriting claims.

I tried to refute this claim and could not. Every factual element matches the primary source, which I read as raw arXiv HTML and not only through a summariser. The source is arXiv:2608.18586v1, "OmniHandwritingOCR" (Guo, Zhang, Jiang, East China Normal University). It was submitted 19 Aug 2026 and is in the CIKM 2026 ACM template (Rome, 7-11 Nov 2026, CC BY 4.0). That is 7 weeks before today (2026-10-08).

(1) Sec. 4.4 says verbatim: "four recurring error patterns: correcting writer mistakes, inserting plausible intermediate steps, dropping visually present but hard-to-read symbols, and drifting into Markdown or explanatory formatting."

(2) The same paragraph says: "error rates above 100 ... DeepSeek-VL2-27B's 133.85 CER on Chinese handwriting and DeepSeek-OCR's 154.81 CER on single-line formulas. Such values mean that insertions dominate the edit distance". It also says "Figure 4 further illustrates cases where models correct students' original mistakes". "Insertions dominate" is the authors' own wording. It also follows mathematically: CER above 100% requires the output to be longer than the reference.

(3) All four numbers are exact in the tables:
- Table 5: DeepSeek-VL2-27B zh-text CER 133.85.
- Table 6: single-line CER 154.81 for DeepSeek-OCR and 116.77 for PaddleOCR-VL.
- Table 4 (entire benchmark): MinerU2.5-1.2B CER 125.59, WER 124.65.

(4) I opened Figure 4 itself. It shows two Chinese student maths solutions. In the hyperbola one, the student wrote y²/9, the ground truth keeps 9, and Qwen2.5-VL-72B outputs 3 and inserts "已知". That is a literal wrong-to-right flip. In the cost-plan one, InternVL3-78B turns 1540 into 15400, rewords the labels and drops a term. The paper's protocol penalises any output that "changes an incorrect formula into a correct one", and its discussion warns about "educational analytics" pipelines that treat OCR text as faithful. So the auto-grader implication is an inference, but it is signposted as one and has a concrete example behind it.

Independent corroboration is arXiv:2608.22959, WildHandBench (24 Aug 2026), from a different team, with 18 newer models. These include Gemini 3.1 Pro and 3.5 Flash, Claude Opus 4.8, Qwen3.5-Plus, Kimi-K3, DeepSeek-OCR-v2 and PaddleOCR-VL-1.6.
- 63-91% of model errors are "prior-driven" (fluent but visually unsupported) against 49% for humans.
- Its appendix shows Gemini "corrects" handwriting to a memorised canonical text and "polishes" a child's essay.
- DeepSeek-OCR-v2 and MinerU-2.5 also fail on wild handwriting with their default prompts (text edit distance 91.7 and 83.8). That answers the worry that the CER above 100% values were only an artifact of OmniHandwritingOCR's single prompt.

Qualifications, none of which amounts to a refutation:
- It is a single v1 preprint, and the promised data and scripts are not yet verified as released.
- The benchmark is deliberately hard. Public samples were kept where Qwen2.5-VL-72B performed poorly (160K cut to 46K), and difficulty scoring uses GPT-4o NED. It also uses one "convert to Markdown" prompt for every model. The CER values are therefore stress-test numbers, not typical error rates.
- The "silent correction" evidence is qualitative, with no frequency given. CER above 100% shows over-generation or runaway output (the authors cap outputs at 128 and 1024 characters), not subtle corrections. The claim keeps these two things separate.
- The 13 models are 2024-25 vintage. GPT-4o is the only closed model, and newer versions such as PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 behave differently.
- Neither paper tests Indic scripts (Chinese, English and LaTeX only).

WebSearch was exhausted (200/200), so I could not search the open web for rebuttals. I checked by direct fetches of the paper, its Figure 4 and the second benchmark, and found nothing that disputes the claim.

The paper gives no per-language or per-scenario results, and reports a single run with no confidence intervals. Its limitations section says the 500 samples "should not be interpreted as a population-level estimate".

4. "Proprietary leaders" is a thin and ageing set. Only three proprietary models were tested and none is from OpenAI. Opus 4.8 scores below three of the four open general models, which the paper does not explain. Kimi's card compares against GPT-5.5, GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Fable 5, none of which were tested here. Google's models page (footer: last updated 2026-10-06) lists Gemini 3.8 Flash as the newest Flash and calls Gemini 3.5 Flash the "legacy" Flash model.

Caveats that qualify the claim but do not falsify it:
1. Authorship. All nine authors are listed as "Baidu Inc." on the PDF title page. Cheng Cui and Changda Zhou also wrote PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 (arXiv 2606.03264), and Qianfan-OCR and Unlimited-OCR are Baidu models. There is no conflict-of-interest statement. The 0.15-point lead over GLM-OCR is noise on 500 images.
2. Internal sloppiness. Appendix Table 5 lists GPT-5.4, which is absent from Table 2, and omits dots.ocr and dots.mocr. Its "DeepSeek-OCR-v2" model ID is deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-OCR, which is the v1 repo; v2 is deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-OCR-2. The language and structure counts also differ between the main text and the appendix (English 143 vs 144; tables 81 vs 79). The 9.46 row may therefore be a wrong-checkpoint or pipeline artefact. In Baidu's own Real5-OmniDocBench table, DeepSeek-OCR 2 scores 73.01. ArXiv 2606.29213 documents DeepSeek-OCR catastrophic repetition failures on Devanagari.
3. Scoring and data mix. Overall weights text, tables and formulas equally, although about 73% of images are free text. About 72% of images are scraped from the internet (calligraphy, archives). Only about 116 of 500 are education or maths/science. General VLMs got the OmniDocBench prompt while OCR models ran their defaults. Ground truth was pre-annotated with 3 MLLMs.
4. No replication. I found no public dataset or code (Hugging Face and GitHub searches empty; the HF paper page returns 404). arXiv search finds no citing or replicating work.
5. No Indic evidence. The paper has none for Assamese, Bengali or Hindi, and the claim must not be extrapolated to them.

Independent work is consistent with the claim, not contradicting it. OmniHandwritingOCR (arXiv 2608.18586, 19 Aug 2026) finds a general MLLM (Qwen3-VL-8B) best in aggregate, with specialists competitive only on subsets. The Devanagari stress test (2606.29213) finds specialised OCR-VLMs the most fragile under degradation. Baidu's own PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 report shows the specialist beating Gemini-3 Pro on printed Real5-OmniDocBench (93.19 vs 89.24), which matches WildHandBench's statement that specialists lead on printed documents and trail on handwriting.

result.evidence:
Checked against the full text of the primary source (arXiv:2608.22959v1, WildHandBench, submitted 24 Aug 2026, the only version, no journal ref). I read it verbatim from arxiv.org/html and the abs page, not from a summary. Every figure in the claim matches Table 2. Overall PDE: GLM-OCR 63.28, PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 64.48, Kimi-K3 71.94, Gemini 3.1 Pro 77.51, Gemini 3.5 Flash 79.21, DeepSeek-OCR2 90.80, Human 49.27. Formula PDE runs 87.83 (PaddleOCR-VL-1.6) to 98.35 (DeepSeek-OCR2), Gemini 3.1 Pro 94.77, Human 46.36. I recomputed all 19 rows: each overall PDE equals the mean of its text, table and formula PDE, so the table is internally consistent. The abstract and introduction say 63-91%. The Conclusion says "63–79% prior-driven for models vs. 49% for humans", and the Discussion applies 63-79% to functional models only. The highest value excluding DeepSeek-OCR2 is 79.21, so the claimed inconsistency is real and unfixed. The PDE definition (segment is prior-driven if its perplexity under Qwen3-8B-Base is lower than the ground truth's; insertions always count), the statement that humans are conservative and partial on illegible text (the appendix shows humans writing a question mark), and both author caveats (error type not error quantity; dependence on the Qwen3-8B-Base reference model) are all in the paper. The ExamLeaf implication is labelled the claimant's own inference, and independent work supports it. Seong et al. 2026 (arXiv:2604.22774) found 15 VLMs fixing students' handwritten maths errors in 42-66% of transcriptions on FERMAT (2,244 samples). The WildHandBench appendix also shows Gemini polishing a child's essay. I found no source that contradicts the claim. The WebSearch budget was exhausted, so counter-search was limited to direct reads of the paper, its abs page and its closest cited work.

Verdict: not refuted. Qualifications the report should carry with it:
(1) The benchmark is 500 images, 66.6% Simplified Chinese and 28.6% English, with only 52 formula images. It has no Indic scripts and no exam answer sheets, so relevance to ExamLeaf is by analogy only.
(2) The authors say the 87-98% formula figure is probably inflated because LaTeX is inherently low-perplexity and even legitimate format differences count as prior-driven. It is therefore not evidence of silent fixing of maths steps.

- The Abstract says "63-91% ... versus only 49% for humans". The Conclusion says "63-79% ... vs. 49%". The next-highest model after DeepSeek-OCR2 is Gemini 3.5 Flash at 79.21, so 63-79 is the range excluding DeepSeek-OCR2. The body ("Error Pattern Analysis") says this range is "among models with functional visual encoders".
