The ExamLeaf implication is labelled as the claimant's own inference. It is plausible and has some support:
- The paper's Appendix Figs 9-10 show Gemini "polishing" a child's essay and a maths derivation.
- An independent paper, Seong et al. (arXiv:2604.22774, Apr 2026), finds VLMs "fix" student errors in multi-line handwritten maths. GPT-4o over-corrects most and Gemini 2.5 Flash is the most faithful.
- Neither paper measures mark inflation.

The claim omits material qualifiers. Anyone reusing it should add these:
1. The authors say formula PDE is "likely because LaTeX syntax is inherently low-perplexity - even legitimate format differences satisfy the ppl criterion". Inserted content is also auto-counted as prior-driven. So 87.83-98.35% overstates fluent substitution, and the formula subset is only 52 images. It is weak support for a "maths step silently fixed" risk.
2. On free text (73% of images), human PDE is 66.96 against model PDEs of 52.59-84.06 (median 68.6). Eight of the 18 models are below the human figure. The 49 vs 63-91 gap comes from the table and formula columns and the 1/3-weight macro-average.
3. DeepSeek-OCR2, the top of the range, scored only 9.46 overall recognition (text edit 91.70, TEDS 1.77). Appendix Table 5 lists its model ID as deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-OCR, which is the v1 repo; v2 is deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-OCR-2. Table 5 also lists GPT-5.4, which is absent from Table 2, and omits Dots.ocr and Dots.mocr, which are in Table 2.
4. The benchmark covers only Simplified Chinese (66.6%), English (28.6%), Traditional Chinese (2.6%) and Chinese-English mixed (2.2%). It has no Indic scripts and no exam scripts. The PDE judge is Qwen3-8B-Base, so it is not portable to Assamese or Bengali.
5. It is an unreviewed single-version preprint with a self-defined metric. Authors Cheng Cui and Changda Zhou also co-authored the PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 report (arXiv:2606.03264), and PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 is an evaluated model that gets the lowest formula PDE and the second-lowest overall PDE. No affiliations or conflict-of-interest statement appear in the arXiv metadata or HTML text.

I recomputed Overall = ((100-Edit)+TEDS+CDM)/3 for all 19 rows and each matches within 0.02. The deltas 1.75 and 3.60 are correct (27.10-26.07 = 1.03). Kimi K3 = 2.8T total / 104B active with released weights, per the abstract of arXiv:2607.24653. The paper gives no price, latency or throughput figures, only config (8192 max output tokens, 120-300 s timeouts).

WHY REFUTED
1. "Proprietary leaders" is wrong. Table 2 has only 3 proprietary models.
- Kimi K3's own report names Claude Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol as the strongest proprietary models and says K3 outperforms Claude Opus 4.8. It cites Artificial Analysis Index v4.1 as of 23 Jul 2026: Fable 5 59.9, GPT-5.6 Sol 58.9, K3 57.1.
- Live OpenRouter listing dates: Claude Fable 5 (2026-06-09), GPT-5.6 Sol (07-09), Gemini 3.6 Flash (07-21) and Claude Opus 5 (07-24). All predate the paper's own 27 Jul 2026 model-access date, and none was tested.
- The paper's appendix Table 5 ("complete list of evaluated models") includes GPT-5.4, but Table 2 omits it. Table 2's Dots.ocr and Dots.mocr are missing from Table 5. English/free-text/table counts differ between the body (143/367/81) and appendix (144/369/79).
- Since then Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Qwen3.8 and GLM-5.3 have shipped. As of 2026-10-08 the comparison is a superseded generation.
2. Strength vs source. The benchmark is 66.6% Simplified Chinese, 28.6% English and 4.8% Traditional Chinese or mixed, with zero Indic scripts. 71.8% of it is scraped from the internet, and the annotators are all native Chinese speakers. It has 52 formula images and 79-81 table images, no confidence intervals and no repeat runs. The authors say it is not a population-level estimate and that the small formula and table subsets lack power to separate close models. The claim leans on 1.03-, 1.75- and 3.60-point gaps. The text metric also rewards format compliance (best model 24.32 beats the human baseline 30.08).
3. Selective emphasis. On formula CDM, the category that matters for maths and chemistry, Kimi-K3 (70.50) trails Gemini 3.1 Pro (79.42) by 8.92. It also trails Claude Opus 4.8 (74.11) and Qwen3.5-Plus (73.77). Qwen3-VL is 9.66 Overall points behind the leader, whereas the paper calls the 5.24-point human-model gap "narrow".
4. "Winners are very large MoE" is unsupported. The proprietary winners have no parameter counts ("-"). In the same table, 241B InternVL3.5 (52.80) loses to 0.9B PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 (54.21) and 0.9B GLM-OCR (54.06). The independent OmniHandwritingOCR (arXiv:2608.18586) has an 8B Qwen3-VL on top and says size does not determine handwriting-OCR quality. "Qwen3.5-Plus" as tested is Alibaba's hosted API model; OpenRouter shows no weights for it, and the open sibling is Qwen3.5-397B-A17B. Also, near-parity is not cheaper: OpenRouter lists Kimi K3 at $0.50/$15 per M tokens vs Gemini 3.5 Flash at $1.50/$9.
5. Source quality. A single unreviewed v1 preprint; all nine authors are listed at Baidu Inc., whose PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 and Qianfan-OCR are in the table. I found no code or data release link in the paper.

result.summary: No OCR or grading system has been tested on ExamLeaf's actual input: phone photos of Assamese, Bengali or Hindi answer sheets with maths and diagrams. The nearest results are poor. The best published score for handwritten Assamese is 71.6% word accuracy (Gemini 3.1 Pro, on a benchmark run by a vendor). Word error on handwritten Hindi and Bengali pages is 3-7% on clean prose with Sarvam OCR or Gemini Flash, and 17-25% on another benchmark. AWS Textract and Azure cannot read Assamese or Bengali, and Google Document AI does not list Assamese. On handwriting, the Chinese OCR specialists (DeepSeek-OCR, PaddleOCR-VL, MinerU, dots.ocr) score below general vision models, even in Chinese and English. Every generative reader also silently 'corrects' student mistakes: 63-79% of errors are of this kind, and 88-95% on formulas. Long handwritten maths is read badly by every model tested, so a transcript can turn a wrong answer into a right one before it is marked. On OpenRouter the best-value Chinese vision model is GLM-5.3-Flash ($0.15/$0.50 per million input/output tokens, $0.06/$0.20 in batch, Artificial Analysis index 41.8). Gemini 3.8 Flash scores 40.9 at $0.75/$3.75. However, Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna cost the same as GLM-5.3-Flash ($0.10/$0.50), and no model has checked evidence on grading accuracy or Assamese. Gemini 2.5 and most Qwen3-VL listings expire this month. OpenRouter's default routing can send children's answer sheets to providers that store data or train on it, unless zdr:true and an allow-list of providers are set. Working from checked prices, the AI cost is about ₹0.2-₹17 per 12-page paper (US$0.002-0.18). The suggested pipeline costs about ₹5.5 per paper, or ₹55-₹170 per student for 20 papers a year. Reading the pages (Sarvam charges ₹0.50 per page) and teacher review cost more than the grading itself. A careful first version would be: practice-only and two-stage, with a word-for-word transcript the student can see; routing restricted to zero-retention endpoints; teacher review of low-confidence answers; a head-to-head test against Sarvam Vision 2.1 and the open IndicOCR model on 100-200 of ExamLeaf's own teacher-marked papers before launch; and a lawyer's review of parental consent under India's data protection law (the DPDP Act) before children's handwriting is sent abroad.

findings.claim: Handwritten Assamese has never been measured on exam answer sheets. The closest evidence puts word error at about 28-34% for the best general systems on handwriting blocks, and about 15% for a recogniser trained for the job on isolated word crops. Assamese reading should be treated as unproven.
findings.evidence: Bodhan AI and AI4Bharat run their own IndicOCR-HW benchmark. The figures are self-reported; the model card was last modified 7 Sep 2026. Their blog describes 10,544 pre-cropped text-block images across 12 Indian languages plus English, with writers from school students to adults. The benchmark is not released and has no exam sheets. Word accuracy is 100 x (1 - WER). Assamese results: Gemini 3.1 Pro 71.6, the open 0.8B IndicOCR 66.1, Sarvam Vision 47.8, Gemma-4-31B 24.1, Chandra OCR 2 8.9, Surya OCR 2 17.8. Gemini 3.1 Pro vs IndicOCR in other languages: Bengali 74.8/71.3, Hindi 83.1/77.6, English 84.4/80.7, overall 72.0/66.7. IndicOCR reads printed Assamese at 90.2, so handwriting is much harder. Gemini beats IndicOCR on 12 of 13 handwriting rows. The Sarvam Vision column predates Sarvam Vision 2.1 (24 Sep 2026), the release that added Indic handwriting, so that figure is likely out of date (my inference from the dates). IIIT-Indic-HW-UC (ICPR 2024): an older-style baseline trained and tested on phone-camera word crops scores Assamese CRR 90.98 / WRR 85.15, Bengali 96.60/89.10 and Hindi 93.88/84.69. That is 11-15% word error even on data like its training data. The writers were adults copying short paragraphs, and the test split is not shown to use new writers. The IIIT page-level paper (IndicPage-OCR, DAS 2026) covers only Hindi, Bengali, Tamil and Telugu. It never mentions Assamese, maths, equations, diagrams or answer scripts, and lists mixed-script pages as future work. Sarvam's Vision 2.1 post claims handwriting support for English plus 22 Indic languages, including Assamese, but shows only demo videos and no accuracy figure. Assamese uses the Bengali Unicode block but has its own letters (U+09F0, U+09F1), so Bengali results are only a rough stand-in.

WildHandBench (arXiv 2608.22959, v1 preprint) uses 500 real-world handwritten documents in Chinese and English. Overall scores: Gemini 3.1 Pro 71.85, Gemini 3.5 Flash 68.25, Kimi-K3 67.81, Qwen3.5-Plus 65.55, Qwen3-VL 62.19, Claude Opus 4.8 57.70; these six are all general models. The best of 11 OCR specialists are PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 (0.9B) 54.21, GLM-OCR 54.06, MinerU2.5-Pro 51.73, HunyuanOCR 51.44, dots.mocr 49.97 and dots.ocr 43.73. DeepSeek-OCR2 scores 9.46, probably a test-setup error: the appendix lists the v1 repository. On free text alone the gap is not uniform: HunyuanOCR (edit distance 38.50) and PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 (41.52) beat Claude Opus 4.8 (53.30). Counter-evidence: EDU-CIRCUIT-HW (ACL 2026 Findings) uses real STEM student handwriting. It ranks Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking last (85.43% sample error) and Gemini-3-Preview first (37.62%). A broader claim that Chinese open models sit close to the proprietary leaders failed verification (1-2).

findings.claim: Every model tested transcribes long, multi-line handwritten maths from real student answer sheets poorly. On the hard tier the best system reaches only 55.81 1-NED, with a character error rate of about 55%.
findings.evidence: OmniHandwritingOCR's multi-line tiers come from more than 6,000 real student maths answer sheets, written in Chinese plus LaTeX. From easy to hard, Qwen3-VL-8B's F1 falls from 86.92 to 70.45 and its CER rises from 24.95 to 57.08. Hard-tier 1-NED/CER: Qwen2.5-VL-72B 55.81/54.91, Qwen3-VL-8B 50.54/57.08, InternVL3-78B 45.59/60.80, DeepSeek-OCR 42.24/70.71, PaddleOCR-VL 41.78/83.51, Nanonets 41.67/67.51, GPT-4o 29.60/75.58. Mean answer length grows from 156.9 to 488.8 characters, LaTeX commands from 4.1 to 25.7, and lines from 3.7 to 13.0. Qualifications: scoring compares LaTeX strings, which penalises equivalent notation. GPT-4o's own errors helped define the hard tier. The dataset is not public. No Gemini, Claude or GPT-5-class model was tested. The direction is backed by Seong et al. (arXiv 2604.22774) and FERMAT (arXiv 2501.07244).

findings.claim: Generative readers 'fix' what the student actually wrote, so a transcription step can turn a wrong answer into a right one before marking. This happens across models and is worst on formulas.
findings.evidence: OmniHandwritingOCR (section 4.4) names four recurring errors: correcting the writer's mistakes, inserting plausible intermediate steps, dropping symbols that are hard to read, and drifting into Markdown or explanation. In Fig. 4, Qwen2.5-VL-72B and InternVL3-78B change a student's y^2/9 to y^2/3 and 1540 to 15400. Some character error rates exceed 100% (output longer than the original): DeepSeek-VL2-27B on Chinese text 133.85, DeepSeek-OCR on single-line formulas 154.81, PaddleOCR-VL 116.77, MinerU2.5 overall 125.59. The single generic prompt may exaggerate these. WildHandBench measures 'prior-driven' errors, where the model writes a more probable string than what is on the page, judged by Qwen3-8B-Base. For working models this is 63.28% of errors (GLM-OCR) to 79.21% (Gemini 3.5 Flash); Gemini 3.1 Pro is 77.51%, against 49.27% for human transcribers. On formulas it is 87.83-94.77% (Gemini 3.1 Pro 94.77%) against 46.36% for humans. Humans tend to mark unreadable text with '?' instead of guessing. This measure describes the type of error, not how many errors there are. Seong et al., 'When VLMs Fix Students' (arXiv 2604.22774), tested 15 models on FERMAT. They found that over-correction hides exactly the mistakes an assessment is meant to catch, with GPT-4o heavily penalised and Gemini 2.5 Flash the most faithful. The effect on marks is an inference: no paper measured inflated scores directly.

findings.claim: Recognisers trained on scanned handwriting fall apart on phone-camera handwriting, and training on camera data restores 38-44 points of word accuracy. ExamLeaf's own phone photos are therefore its most valuable data for testing and training.
findings.evidence: IIIT-Indic-HW-UC, Table 3 (ICPR 2024). Trained on the older scanned set and tested on camera images: Bengali WRR falls from 84.29 to 51.51 (CRR 95.72 to 79.66), and Hindi from 83.09 to 40.81 (CRR 96.08 to 72.27). Trained on camera data: Bengali 89.10 and Hindi 84.69, but accuracy on the old set drops to 53.82 and 63.65. Training on both sets is best on both. Other languages drop more (Malayalam 89.78 to 32.07, Tamil 92.19 to 41.24). Assamese exists only in the camera set (WRR 85.15). Confounds: camera conditions are mixed up with writer and content differences; the data are word crops from adults aged mostly 20-40; and the recogniser is an older-style baseline. The dataset and code were promised 'after acceptance' and the links are dead. A 2026 preprint (arXiv 2606.29213) found 9 of 10 OCR systems collapse on real Hindi scans: GPT-5.5 scored chrF++ 58.5 against 86.3 for Gemini 2.5 Flash.

findings.claim: On OpenRouter (8 Oct 2026) the best-value Chinese vision models are GLM-5.3-Flash and MiMo-V2.6-Pro. Western models are now just as cheap (Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna at $0.10/$0.50), so 'Chinese means cheaper' no longer holds. No model has checked evidence on exam grading or Assamese.
findings.vote: 3-0 on claim [15]; batch prices and other entries are a synthesizer re-fetch of the same catalogue
findings.evidence: Prices are per million input/output tokens. AA is the Artificial Analysis intelligence index: a general-intelligence score measured at maximum reasoning effort, not a grading or handwriting test. z-ai/glm-5.3-flash: $0.15/$0.50, AA 41.8, text+image+video input, 1M context, reasoning mandatory with default effort 'max' (efforts max/high/low), batch $0.06/$0.20. xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-pro: $0.435/$0.87, AA 46.3, text+image+video+audio. deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash: $0.30/$1.20, AA 39.5, text+image, batch $0.112/$0.336. moonshotai/kimi-k3: $0.50/$15, AA 43.6, but most endpoints charge $3/$15. qwen/qwen3.7-flash: $0.03/$0.13 with size tiers, and qwen3.8-flash: $0.15/$0.47; neither has an AA score. qwen/qwen3-vl-235b-a22b-instruct: $0.21/$1.90, AA 9.9. minimax-m3: $0.30/$1.20, AA 29.2. stepfun step-3.7-flash: $0.20/$1.15, AA 19.5. tencent/hy3 and hunyuan-a13b take text only. Western models: google/gemini-3.8-flash $0.75/$3.75, AA 40.9 (39.8 at default effort), batch $0.375/$1.875. google/gemini-3.1-pro-preview $2/$12. openai/gpt-6-luna $0.10/$0.50, AA 38.1 (29.9 at default), batch $0.05/$0.25. anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 $0.10/$0.50, AA 43.4 at max and 34.5 at default per the AA site, batch $0.05/$0.25. anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5 $2/$10, AA 56 (46.8 at default). AA's measured cost per task: GLM-5.3-Flash $0.253 (68.7K output tokens, 46.6K of them reasoning), Gemini 3.8 Flash $1.243, MiMo $0.133, Haiku 5.5 $0.213. No Sarvam model (including Sarvam-M) is listed on OpenRouter.

findings.claim: Several models named in the original brief are being retired. On OpenRouter, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Flash-Lite and Pro expire on 20 Oct 2026 and five Qwen3-VL variants on 9 Oct 2026. The two Qwen3-VL listings that remain score only 9.9 and 7.9 on the AA index, against 41.8 for GLM-5.3-Flash.
findings.evidence: 32 catalogue entries carry an expiration date. google/gemini-2.5-flash, -flash-lite and -pro, plus the flash and pro batch versions, expire 2026-10-20. qwen3-vl-8b-instruct, 32b-instruct, 8b-thinking, 30b-a3b-thinking and 235b-a22b-thinking expire 2026-10-09. baidu/ernie-4.5-vl expires 2026-10-08. A synthesizer check also found qwen3.5-9b expiring 21 Oct and qwen3.6-max-preview 9 Oct. Google's Vertex AI lifecycle page lists Gemini 2.5 retirement on 20 Oct 2026, with replacements Gemini 3.8 Flash, 3.5 Flash, 3.5 Flash-Lite and 3.1 Flash-Lite. AI Studio still serves 2.5 to existing users only. Alibaba's deprecation notices fall at 10 Oct 00:00 UTC+8. Qwen3-VL's open weights remain available and are still hosted by Parasail, DeepInfra and Novita. 'Expiration date' means the model may be removed after that date. The practical point: pin exact model versions, keep a fixed test set, and re-check accuracy whenever a model is swapped.

findings.claim: Headline prices come with conditions. Prompt-size tiers bill the whole request at the higher rate. Some providers charge differently by time of day. Batch versions cut 50-72%.
findings.vote: 3-0 on claim [17]; batch prices and Gemini token counts are a synthesizer check
findings.evidence: qwen/qwen3.7-flash costs $0.03/$0.13, rising to $0.10/$0.40 above 32K prompt tokens and $0.20/$0.80 above 256K. Alibaba bills all tokens in the request at that tier. Qwen counts one token per 32x32 pixels, with 2,560 tokens per image by default and up to 16,384 at high resolution. So 12 pages (about 30.7K tokens) plus a 5K-token prompt comes to 35.7K and crosses the 32K line. That costs $0.0088, against $0.0026 for the same call with images shrunk to about 2,000 tokens each: 3.4 times as much. anthropic/claude-haiku-5.5 rises from $0.10/$0.50 to $0.50/$2.50 above 100K tokens. tencent/hy3 on Tencent's own endpoint costs $0.132/$0.528 from 00:00 to 16:00 UTC and $0.0825/$0.33 otherwise. deepseek-v4-pro-0813 on DeepSeek's endpoint costs $1.32/$3.96 on weekdays 01:00-04:00 and 06:00-10:00 UTC, and $0.66/$1.98 otherwise. 83 of 467 catalogue entries carry such conditions. Batch versions: glm-5.3-flash:batch $0.06/$0.20 (60% off). gemini-3.8-flash:batch 50% off. deepseek-v4.1-flash:batch $0.112/$0.336 (63% off input, 72% off output). claude-haiku-5.5:batch and gpt-6-luna:batch $0.05/$0.25 (50% off). kimi-k3:batch costs $2.28/$11.40, more than its cheapest normal endpoint. Gemini image tokens per page (docs updated 23 Sep 2026): 1,120 at default/high, 280 low, 560 medium, 2,240 ultra_high. Reasoning tokens are billed as output.

findings.claim: OpenRouter's default routing (data_collection: allow) can send children's answer sheets to providers that store prompts or train on them. Protecting them needs zdr:true, data_collection:deny and an allow-list of providers. The cheapest Qwen Flash models have no zero-retention endpoint at all.
findings.vote: 3-0 on claims [18], [19]; ZDR endpoint list is a synthesizer check
findings.evidence: OpenRouter's docs say data_collection defaults to 'allow', which permits providers that store user data and may train on it. 'deny' restricts routing to providers that do not collect data. zdr:true routes only to endpoints with a Zero Data Retention (ZDR) policy. It is combined with account-wide, model-group and guardrail settings, and can only tighten them, never loosen them. OpenRouter's provider list (8 Oct 2026) flags 4 providers as training on data, including DeepSeek, and 39 as retaining prompts, including Google AI Studio (55 days), Anthropic (30 days), Xiaomi (30 days), Alibaba Cloud International, MiniMax and OpenAI. The FAQ says training providers are skipped unless an account setting is switched on. The ZDR endpoint list (945 endpoints) shows: GLM-5.3-Flash on 29 endpoints including Z.AI, DeepInfra, Together and Fireworks. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on 23 third-party hosts, but not DeepSeek's own. MiMo-V2.6-Pro on Novita and DeepInfra. Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.1 Pro on Google. Claude Haiku 5.5 on Google and Amazon Bedrock. GPT-6 Luna on Azure. Qwen3-VL-235B on Venice, DeepInfra, Parasail and Novita. Qwen3.7-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash: none. Whether each ZDR endpoint accepts images was not checked. ZDR does not mean data stays in India: OpenRouter's in-region routing covers only the EU and US. A BYOK key's 'declared_zdr' is self-declared, and ZDR does not cover plugins or tools.

findings.claim: Using the checked prices, the AI cost of marking a 12-page, 30-question paper is about ₹0.2-₹17 (US$0.002-0.18), and ₹19-₹53 if Gemini 3.1 Pro does everything. The suggested pipeline costs about ₹5.5 per paper, or ₹55-₹170 per student for 20 papers a year. Reading the pages and teacher review cost more than the grading model.
findings.vote: n/a: synthesizer arithmetic on the prices verified in claims [15], [17] and on prices checked separately
findings.evidence: Assumptions: the 3,000-word marking scheme is about 4,000 tokens, plus 1,000 for instructions. The transcript is about 10,000 tokens, because Indic scripts use many tokens per word. Image tokens per page: Gemini 1,120 (high), Qwen 2,560 (default limit), others assumed 1,500. Output is 3,000 visible tokens (about 100 per question) plus 0, 10K or 40K reasoning tokens. Exchange rate ₹96.7 per US$ (ECB reference rate, 7 Oct 2026). Single-step grading straight from the page images, at low/mid/high reasoning: Gemini 3.8 Flash ₹2.43 / ₹6.05 / ₹16.93 (batch ₹1.21 / ₹3.03 / ₹8.47). Gemini 3.1 Pro ₹7.05 / ₹18.65 / ₹53.46. GLM-5.3-Flash ₹0.48 / ₹0.96 / ₹2.41 (batch ₹0.19 / ₹0.38 / ₹0.97). DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ₹1.02 / ₹2.18 / ₹5.66 (batch ₹0.35-₹1.65). Claude Haiku 5.5 or GPT-6 Luna ₹0.37 / ₹0.85 / ₹2.30. Qwen3.7-Flash ₹0.46 / ₹0.85 / ₹2.01, because it crosses the 32K price tier. Reading stage per paper: Sarvam Digitisation ₹6.00 ($0.062). Google Document AI ₹1.74 ($0.018). Gemini 3.8 Flash as transcriber ₹4.64 (batch ₹2.32). Gemini 3.1 Pro ₹14.30. Qwen3.7-Flash ₹0.22. Text grading after transcription: GLM-5.3-Flash ₹0.36 / ₹0.85 / ₹2.30; Gemini 3.8 Flash ₹2.18 / ₹5.80 / ₹16.68; Qwen3.7-Flash ₹0.08-₹0.58. Suggested two-stage pipeline (Gemini 3.8 Flash transcript plus GLM-5.3-Flash grading at mid reasoning): about ₹5.5 per paper ($0.057), about ₹2.7 in batch, and about ₹8.4 if 20% of pages are re-read by Gemini 3.1 Pro. At an assumed 20 papers per student per year, that is ₹55-₹170. Illustration only: if 6 of 30 answers go to a teacher at 30 seconds each and ₹300 per hour, review costs about ₹15 per paper, more than all the AI costs combined. Translating comments with Sarvam (₹0.005 per character) would cost ₹15-₹25 for 3,000-5,000 characters. Having the grader write comments directly in Assamese, Bengali or Hindi only adds output tokens. Caching the shared marking scheme (cached input is 10 times cheaper) saves little in absolute terms.

findings.claim: Adding Assamese or another Indic language 'easily' only works with open-weight models: fine-tune IndicOCR-class or GOT-OCR models with LoRA on your own phone photos. Commercial APIs come with a fixed language list. Feedback in the student's language is easiest to get by having the grader write it directly.
findings.vote: 3-0 on claims [0], [1], [3], [4]; Sarvam translation price is a synthesizer check
findings.evidence: There are three places a language can be added. 1. Reading. IndicPage-OCR trains one adapter per language on GOT-OCR 2.0. Adapters for Hindi, Bengali, Tamil and Telugu are public (Apache-2.0, Hugging Face SHAON123/indicpage-ocr-*); there is none for Assamese, and the code is 'coming soon'. Training used about 12M augmented word and line crops plus thousands of pages per language (for example 23,912 Hindi and 7,189 Bengali pages). The exact recipe and compute claim failed verification (1-2), but the data volume suggests labelled data, not GPUs, is the bottleneck. Bodhan IndicOCR (Qwen3.5-0.8B plus a 33M layout model, built with AI4Bharat) reads handwriting in English plus 12 Indian languages including Assamese. It is gated under a custom 'Indic Open Model License v1.0', so check commercial and fine-tuning terms; MLX and ONNX conversions exist. Training on phone-camera data matters a lot (38-44 WRR points, see the camera finding). Datasets: IIIT-Indic-HW-UC is camera-captured and includes Assamese, about 200K word images per language, but its release status is unclear. IIIT-INDIC-HW-WORDS is scanned and has no Assamese. Commercial APIs cannot be extended: Sarvam covers 22 Indic languages plus English; Google Document AI handwriting covers Bengali, Hindi, Marathi and Nepali; Cloud Vision has Assamese as experimental; Textract and Azure do not. 2. Grading. The prompt and marking scheme can be in any language, but Indic text uses more tokens. 3. Feedback. Sarvam translation costs ₹0.005 per character (₹0.004 on the Business plan), and Sarvam has a Dubbing API. Generating comments directly is cheaper. There is no checked evidence on how well GLM or Gemini write Assamese.

findings.claim: Recommended first version, based on the evidence (this is the synthesizer's judgement, not a tested result). Run a two-stage, practice-only pipeline. Stage one: Gemini 3.8 Flash produces a word-for-word transcript, with low-confidence pages sent to Gemini 3.1 Pro, and the transcript is shown to the student. Stage two: GLM-5.3-Flash (or Gemini 3.8 Flash) grades it against the marking scheme. Route through OpenRouter with zdr:true, data_collection:deny and a provider allow-list. Before launch, test against ExamLeaf's own teacher-marked papers, with Sarvam Vision 2.1 and IndicOCR as the challengers.
findings.evidence: (1) Why two stages and not one. No checked evidence compares grading straight from the image with transcribing first. But silent correction can only be caught if the transcript is visible. A visible transcript lets the student or teacher flag misreads, lets ExamLeaf replace the reader and the grader separately as models expire, and costs only a few rupees more. Instruct the reader to transcribe word for word, keep the student's errors, write [?] for unreadable text instead of guessing, and split the output by question. (2) Reader. Use Gemini 3.8 Flash at high resolution (1,120 tokens per page). Send pages with many [?] marks to Gemini 3.1 Pro, the best measured reader of handwritten Assamese at 71.6% (note it is a preview model). Gemini was near the top on every handwriting test where it appeared in this research (Bodhan Indic, IIIT pages, WildHandBench, EDU-CIRCUIT-HW), and Gemini 2.5 Flash was the most faithful transcriber in Seong et al. Compare it with Sarvam Vision 2.1 Digitise (₹0.50 per page, Indian vendor, handwriting accuracy unpublished) and a self-hosted IndicOCR on ExamLeaf's own pages before committing. (3) Grader. If a Chinese model is wanted, use GLM-5.3-Flash: AA 41.8 at $0.15/$0.50, 29 ZDR endpoints including Z.AI, batch at $0.06/$0.20. Set its reasoning effort explicitly. Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna are alternatives in the same price band. Choose by agreement with teachers' marks, not by AA score. Avoid DeepSeek's own endpoint (it trains on data), Qwen3.7/3.8-Flash (no ZDR endpoint), Kimi K3 ($15 per million output tokens), the Gemini 2.5 and Qwen3-VL listings (expiring), Textract and Azure (no Assamese or Bengali), and Chinese OCR specialists for Indic scripts (no evidence, and they trail general models on handwriting). (4) Route. For a first version, use OpenRouter with zdr:true, data_collection:'deny', an explicit provider allow-list, exact model versions and account-wide ZDR. OpenRouter cannot keep data in India. If a lawyer says data must stay in India, use Google Vertex or Document AI in asia-south1 (Mumbai), use Sarvam directly, or self-host open models on an Indian GPU cloud; self-hosting costs were not established. (5) Product. Practice mode only, with marks labelled as estimates and a confidence level per answer. Send low-confidence, illegible, diagram and chemical-equation answers to a teacher review queue. Give students an appeal button. Before each release, require agreement with teachers on a held-out set of 100-200 marked papers per subject and language. (6) Consent. examleaf-web already records parental consent: accounts/models.py has parent_name, parent_contact and consent_at, plus a ConsentRecord model described as 'One consent event (DPDP Act)'. Extend the privacy notice to name AI processing of handwriting by named processors abroad, and get legal review. Cost: about ₹5.5 per paper in real time, ₹2.7 in batch and ₹8.4 with Pro re-reads, or ₹55-₹170 per student per year.

findings.claim: Risks the founder may not have considered: transcription that silently improves answers, frequent model retirements, unsafe default data routing, price jumps at size thresholds, runaway reasoning tokens, unmeasured accuracy for Assamese and diagrams, benchmarks run by vendors, and API rate limits at exam-season peaks.
findings.vote: 3-0 on the underlying claims; throughput arithmetic and design points are synthesizer inferences
findings.evidence: (a) Readers rewrite student errors into correct answers: 63-79% of errors are of this kind, and 88-95% on formulas, so marks can be inflated without any sign. (b) Model churn: 32 OpenRouter entries are expiring, some within 1-12 days of 8 Oct 2026, so an accuracy check done in one month may not hold the next. (c) OpenRouter's default data_collection 'allow' permits storing and training providers, and the cheapest Qwen Flash models have no ZDR endpoint. (d) Twelve page images can push a request past the 32K tier, costing 3.4 times as much on Qwen3.7-Flash. (e) GLM-5.3-Flash defaults to maximum reasoning: AA measured 46.6K reasoning tokens per task, all billed as output. (f) Nobody has measured Assamese exam handwriting, diagrams, chemical equations or crossed-out work. Readers trained mostly on Bengali may output Bengali র/ব instead of the Assamese letters ৰ/ৱ, so keywords would not match the marking scheme (inference). (g) The main benchmarks are run by vendors and change over time: Sarvam's was rewritten twice, and Bodhan's Sarvam figures predate Sarvam Vision 2.1. (h) Throughput: Sarvam Digitise allows 10 pages per job and 10 requests per minute. A 12-page paper needs 2 jobs, so one account can handle about 300 papers per hour or 7,200 per day unless enterprise limits are higher. OpenRouter's limits and batch turnaround times were not checked. (i) Gemini 3.1 Pro is a preview model. (j) IndicOCR uses a custom gated licence, not an OSI-approved open-source licence. (k) Using students' sheets to fine-tune models needs consent that covers it. (l) If transcripts can be edited and marks ever count for anything beyond practice, students can type in what they did not write. Lock the transcript and show the page image beside it (design inference). (m) Leniency, bias and invented marks were not measured for any grading model.

openQuestions: On 100-200 of ExamLeaf's own phone photos of Assamese, Bengali and Hindi answer pages, with teacher-checked transcripts, what character and word error rates do Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Sarvam Vision 2.1, Bodhan IndicOCR and GLM-5.3-Flash actually reach? How often does each silently correct student mistakes, especially in maths, chemical equations and the Assamese-only letters ৰ and ৱ?

How closely do LLM marks agree with experienced Assam board examiners for each question type (exact and within-one-mark agreement, quadratic weighted kappa, leniency and bias by language)? Does grading straight from the page image beat transcribing first and then grading the text?

What exactly do the DPDP Act 2023 and its Rules require for processing under-18 students' handwritten sheets through foreign AI processors: consent wording, cross-border transfer, processor contracts and retention? What would options that keep data in India cost per paper: Vertex or Document AI in asia-south1, Sarvam direct, or self-hosting on E2E Networks or Yotta?

What accuracy, prices and failure modes do existing AI answer-sheet checkers report (Indian startups, Gradescope-style tools, CBSE or state-board on-screen marking pilots)? What have boards and teacher bodies said about AI marking?
